Yang Hong, courtesy name Jixiu, came from Wuyang in Qianwei. Under Liu Zhang he had served in several commanderies. After the First Lord conquered Shu, Prefect Li Yan named him merit assessor. Li Yan wanted to relocate the prefectural seat. Hong argued fiercely and was ignored, so he resigned as merit assessor and asked to step down. Yan (wished to) recommended Hong to the province as (the post was adjutant for the Shu section) [adjutant for the Shu section]. During the struggle for Hanzhong the First Lord sent urgent orders for reinforcements. Zhuge Liang, as army adviser general, asked Hong's view. Hong said, "Hanzhong is Yi Province's windpipe; on it hangs survival. Lose Hanzhong and Shu cannot stand— this is a disaster on our own doorstep. For this crisis every man should bear arms and every woman should haul supplies— why should we hesitate to mobilize?" Fa Zheng, prefect of Shu, had gone north with the First Lord, so Liang memorialized Hong as acting prefect of Shu. Hong cleared every item of business and was soon confirmed in the post. Before long he was shifted to adjutant for Yi Province administration.

五年，丞相亮北住漢中，欲用張裔為留府長史，問洪何如？洪對曰：「裔天姿明察，長於治劇，才誠堪之，然性不公平，恐不可專任，不如留向朗。朗情偽差少，裔隨從目下，效其器能，於事兩善。」初，裔少與洪親善。裔流放在吳，洪臨裔郡，裔子郁給郡吏，微過受罰，不特原假。裔後還聞之，深以為恨，與洪情好有損。及洪見亮出，至裔許，具說所言。裔答洪曰：「公留我了矣，明府不能止。」時人或疑洪意自欲作長史，或疑洪知裔自嫌，不願裔處要職，典後事也。後裔與司鹽校尉岑述不和，至於忿恨。亮與裔書曰：「君昔在[陌]下，營壞，吾之用心，食不知味；後流洪迸南海，相為悲歎，寢不安席；及其來還，委付大任，同獎王室，自以為與君古之石交也。石交之道，舉仇以相益，割骨肉以相明，猶不相謝也，況吾但委意於元儉，而君不能忍邪？」論者由是明洪無私。

In the fifth year of Jianxing, while Chancellor Liang was stationed north at Hanzhong, he meant to appoint Zhang Yi chief clerk of the rear headquarters and asked Hong what he thought? Hong answered, "Zhang Yi is brilliant and sees through detail; he shines at knotty administration and could fill the role, but he is not evenhanded. I would not give him sole charge— better keep Xiang Lang in place. Xiang Lang is steadier in judgment, while Yi stays close at hand where you can test his capacity— both arrangements serve you well." In their youth Zhang Yi and Yang Hong had been close friends. Later Yi languished in exile in Wu. When Hong became prefect of Yi's old commandery, Yi's son Zhang Yu served as a clerk there; Yu committed a minor offense and Hong punished him without special leniency. When Yi eventually came home and learned of it, he nursed a deep grudge, and the bond between him and Hong cooled. After Liang set out for the front, Hong visited Yi and repeated word for word what he had told the chancellor. Yi told Hong, "The chancellor has already settled on me; our worthy prefect cannot change that. Some thought Hong angled for the chief clerkship himself; others thought he knew Yi resented him and meant to block Yi from a powerful rear post. Later Zhang Yi and Cen Shu, the colonel director of the salt monopoly, fell into a feud that turned venomous. Liang wrote to Yi: "When you were trapped below the Deyang plain and your camp was shattered, I was so anxious I could not taste my food; when you were driven off toward the southern seas we mourned for each other and lay awake at night; and when you returned to a great trust and we worked together for the house of Han, I believed we shared the kind of bond ancients called a friendship carved in stone. Such friends recommend even a personal enemy if it helps the other, or cut kin asunder to prove good faith— and still feel no debt. Can you not bear the fact that I merely leaned on Yang Hong for advice?" Onlookers realized then that Hong had acted without private motive.
洪少不好學問，而忠清款亮，憂公如家，事繼母至孝。六年卒官。始洪為李嚴功曹，嚴未（至）[去]犍為而洪已為蜀郡。

Hong had never cared much for scholarship, but he was loyal, honest, and transparent, treating public duty as family duty and honoring his stepmother with utmost filial piety. He died in office in the sixth year of Jianxing. When Hong first served Li Yan as merit assessor, Yan had not yet (reached) [left] Jianwei when Hong was already administrator of Shu.

洪迎門下書佐何祗，有才策功干，舉郡吏，數年為廣漢太守，時洪亦尚在蜀郡。是以西土鹹服諸葛亮能盡時人之器用也。〈益部耆旧传杂记曰：每朝会，祗次洪坐。嘲祗曰：“君马何驶？”祗曰：“故吏马不敢驶，但明府未著鞭耳。”众传之以为笑。祗字君肃，少寒贫，为人宽厚通济，体甚壮大，又能饮食，好声色，不持节俭，故时人少贵之者。尝梦井中生桑，以问占梦赵直，直曰：“桑非井中之物，会当移植；然桑字四十下八，君寿恐不过此。”祗笑言“得此足矣”。初仕郡，后为督军从事。时诸葛亮用法峻密，阴闻祗游戏放纵，不勤所职，尝奄往录狱。众人咸为祗惧。祗密闻之，夜张灯火见囚，读诸解状。诸葛晨往，祗悉已闇诵，答对解释，无所凝滞，亮甚异之。出补成都令，时郫县令缺，以祗兼二县。二县户口猥多，切近都治，饶诸奸秽，每比人，常眠睡，值其觉寤，辄得奸诈，众咸畏祗之发摘，或以为有术，无敢欺者。使人投算，祗听其读而心计之，不差升合，其精如此。汶山夷不安，以祗为汶山太守，民夷服信。迁广汉。后夷反叛，辞“令得前何府君，乃能安我耳”！时难屈祗，拔祗族人为，汶山复得安。转祗为犍为。年四十八卒，如直所言。后有广汉王离，字伯元，亦以才幹显。为督军从事，推法平当，稍迁，代祗为犍为太守，治有美绩，虽聪明不及祗，而文采过之也。〉

Hong had taken on his clerk He Zhi, a man of plans and practical gifts, and raised him to commandery clerk. Within a few years Zhi was prefect of Guanghan while Hong still governed Shu. People across the west agreed that Zhuge Liang knew how to place every man according to his gifts. The assorted records of the elders of Yi note that at each court session Zhi sat next to Hong. Hong teased him, "Why is your horse so fast today?" Zhi shot back, "A former clerk's horse does not dare bolt— unless his lord has not yet raised the crop." The story spread and became a standing joke. He Zhi, courtesy name Junsu, grew up in bitter poverty yet was openhanded and accommodating. He was a big man with a big appetite and a taste for music and women, careless of thrift, so contemporaries thought little of him. He once dreamed mulberries sprouting in a well and asked the diviner Zhao Zhi to interpret it. Zhao said, "Mulberries do not belong in a well; the omen points to a change of post; yet the graph for “mulberry” breaks into “forty-eight”— I fear you will not live past forty-eight." Zhi laughed and said, "If I get that far, I shall be content." He began in the prefectural office, then became supervising army adjutant. Zhuge Liang's justice was strict. Hearing that Zhi idled and caroused instead of tending his duties, Liang once descended on the jail without warning to review the dockets. Everyone feared for him. Zhi got wind of the visit. That night he lit the lamps, went through the cells, and read every plea and defense. When Liang arrived at dawn, Zhi had memorized the files verbatim, answered every question without hesitation, and left Liang astonished. He was posted out as magistrate of Chengdu while the Pi seat stood empty, so he held both counties at once. Both counties were populous, hugging the capital, and riddled with sharp practice. During hearings Zhi often appeared to doze; the moment a suspect woke to the trap, Zhi had caught the lie. People dreaded his knack for exposure; some swore he used magic— no one dared cheat him. When clerks called out figures from the counting board, he listened and ran the totals in his head without missing a single measure— such was his precision. When the Wenshan tribes grew restless, Zhi was sent as their prefect; Han and native alike trusted him. He was moved to Guanghan. They rose again, insisting, "Bring back the former Prefect He as before or we will not be quiet!" Since Zhi could not be moved without trouble, a kinsman of his was promoted to the vacancy and Wenshan calmed down again. Zhi was then shifted to Qianwei. He died at forty-eight, exactly as Zhao Zhi had foretold. Later Wang Li of Guanghan, courtesy name Boyuan, likewise won renown for his executive ability. He rose through supervising army adjutant, earned a reputation for fair adjudication, and eventually succeeded He Zhi as prefect of Qianwei with a distinguished tenure. He lacked Zhi's lightning mind but outshone him in literary grace.

費詩字公舉，犍為南安人也。劉璋時為綿竹令，先主攻綿竹時，詩先舉城降。成都既定，先主領益州牧，以詩為督軍從事，出為牂牁太守，還為州前部司馬。先主為漢中王，遣詩拜關羽為前將軍，羽聞黃忠為後將軍，（羽）怒曰：「大丈夫終不與老兵同列！」不肯受拜。詩謂羽曰：「夫立王業者，所用非一。昔蕭、曹與高祖少小親舊，而陳、韓亡命後主，論其班列，韓最居上，未聞蕭、曹以此為怨。今（漢王）[漢中王]以一時之功隆崇於漢升，然意之輕重，寧當與君侯齊乎！且王與君侯臂猶一體，同休等戚，禍福共之，愚為君侯不宜計官號之高下、爵祿之多少為意也。僕一介之使，銜命之人，君侯不受拜，如是便還，但相為惜此舉動，恐有後悔耳！」羽大感悟，遂即受拜。

Fei Shi, whose courtesy name was Gongju, came from Nanan in Qianwei. Under Liu Zhang he governed Mianzhu. When the First Lord besieged the town, Shi was first to open the gates and submit. Once Chengdu fell, the First Lord assumed stewardship of Yi Province, named Shi supervising army adjutant, posted him to Zangke, then brought him back as the province's forward army marshal. After the First Lord declared himself king of Hanzhong, he dispatched Shi to present Guan Yu with the commission of forward general. When Yu learned that Huang Zhong had been made rear general, (Guan Yu) he fumed, "A true man does not end his career ranked beside some weather-beaten veteran!" He refused to accept the appointment. Shi told him, "Building an empire takes more than one sort of talent. Long ago Xiao He and Cao Can grew up with Gaozu, whereas Chen He and Han Xin joined him later as fugitive adventurers; when ranks were fixed, Han Xin stood at the top, yet Xiao and Cao raised no complaint. Today (the Prince of Han) [The king of Hanzhong] has exalted Hansheng for one battle, but in the ruler's heart your place still outweighs his— can you doubt it? Besides, you and the king are limb and body, bound in the same fortune; it ill becomes you, my lord, to fuss over who ranks higher or who earns more. I am only a courier with orders in my sleeve. If you refuse the seal, I must ride home empty-handed— and both of us may rue what pride has cost you!" Guan Yu took the point, accepted the commission, and the crisis passed.

後群臣議欲推漢中王稱尊號，詩上疏曰：「殿下以曹操父子逼主篡位，故乃羈旅萬里，糾合士眾，將以討賊。今天敵未克，而先主自立，恐人心疑惑。昔高祖與楚約，先破秦者王。及屠咸陽，獲子嬰，猶懷推讓，況今殿下未出門庭，便欲自立邪！愚臣誠不為殿下取也。」由是忤指，左遷部永昌從事。〈习凿齿曰：夫创本之君，须大定而后正己，纂统之主，俟速建以系众心，是故惠公朝虏而子圉夕立，更始尚存而光武举号，夫岂忘主徼利，社稷之故也。今先主纠合义兵，将以讨贼。贼强祸大，主没国丧，二祖之庙，绝而不祀，苟非亲贤，孰能绍此？嗣祖配天，非咸阳之譬，杖正讨逆，何推让之有？於此时也，不知速尊有德以奉大统，使民欣反正，世睹旧物，杖顺者齐心，附逆者同惧，可谓闇惑矣。其黜降也宜哉！臣松之以为凿齿论议，惟此论最善。〉

When the court began to urge the Prince of Hanzhong to take the imperial title, Shi memorialized: "You left home because the Caos coerced the emperor and stole the mandate; you crossed a thousand leagues to gather an army meant to destroy rebels. Heaven's great foe is still unbeaten, yet you would elevate yourself first— the people will only grow doubtful of your purpose. Remember how Gaozu bargained with Chu that whoever broke Qin first would take the kingship. Even after he stormed Xianyang and held the surrendered emperor, he still hung back from claiming the throne. How can you, who have not yet left your own courtyard, leap ahead to crown yourself?" This is a step your servant cannot in good conscience endorse. For that bluntness he was demoted to adjutant for the Yongchang office. Xi Zuochi argues that a dynastic founder waits until the realm is settled before claiming supreme style, whereas a restorer must move quickly to steady the people— hence Jin Hui Gong could be taken captive at dawn while his heir Ziyu was enthroned that same night, or Guangwu could raise his banner while Gengshi still sat on the throne. Their haste served the altars of state, not private ambition. Here the First Lord has raised a loyal host to strike the usurper. The rebel still towers over us; the Son of Heaven is gone and the dynasty mourns; the twin shrines stand empty. If not for a worthy of the blood, who could renew the line? Continuing the ancestral cult is not the same as Gaozus polite pause at Xianyang; you march under the banner of legitimacy— there is no call for false modesty now. Yet instead of enthroning the worthiest man to reunite the mandate, letting the people see the old order restored and the wavering rally while traitors tremble, you hesitate— that is sheer muddle. Small wonder Fei Shi was cast down! Pei Songzhi remarks that of all Xi Zuochi's opinions, this one alone hits the mark.

建興三年，隨諸葛亮南行，歸至漢陽縣，降人李鴻來詣亮，亮見鴻，時蔣琬與詩在坐。鴻曰：「聞過孟達許，適見王沖從南來，言往者達之去就，明公切齒，欲誅達妻子，賴先主不聽言。達曰：『諸葛亮見顧有本末，終不爾也。』盡不信沖言，委仰明公，無復已已。」亮謂琬、詩曰：「還都當有書與子度相聞。」詩進曰：「孟達小子，昔事振威不忠，後又背叛先主，反覆之人，何足與書邪！」亮默然不答。亮欲誘達以為外援，竟與達書曰：「往年南征，歲（未及）[末及]還，適與李鴻會於漢陽，承知消息，慨然永歎，以存足下平素之志，豈徒空托名榮，貴為乘離乎！嗚呼孟子，斯實劉封侵陵足下，以傷先主待士之義。又鴻道王沖造作虛語，云足下量度吾心，不受沖說。尋表明之言，追平生之好，依依東望，故遣有書。」達得亮書，數相交通，辭欲叛魏。魏遣司馬宣王征之，即斬滅達。亮亦以達無款誠之心，故不救助也。蔣琬秉政，以詩為諫議大夫，卒於家。

In the third year of Jianxing he accompanied Liang on the southern expedition. On the way back they stopped at Hanyang, where the defector Li Hong sought an audience. Liang received him while Jiang Wan and Fei Shi sat in. Hong said, "I stopped at Meng Da's camp and met Wang Chong riding north. Chong told how, when Da first changed sides, you gnashed your teeth and meant to execute his family until the First Lord forbade it. Da answered that Zhuge Liang had always treated him fairly and would never go that far. He put no faith in Chong's story and still places his whole trust in you, my lord— without reserve." Liang told Wan and Shi, "Once we are back in Chengdu I shall write to Zidu to reopen contact." Shi broke in: "Meng Da is a faithless wretch who betrayed Liu Zhang and then our sovereign. A man like that does not deserve a letter from you!" Liang said nothing. Still hoping to win Da as an ally beyond the border, Liang finally wrote: "During the last southern expedition the year closed (before I could) [before I could] return I met Li Hong at Hanyang. His news moved me deeply, for I know the purpose you once avowed— surely you do not mean to cling to hollow titles while we remain sundered!" Alas, my friend, Liu Feng's bullying of you was what soured the First Lord's faith in treating men generously. Hong also said Wang Chong invented rumors, yet you read my heart and refused to believe him. Trusting the plain words of my earlier memorial and the friendship we once shared, I gaze eastward and send this note. Once the letter reached him, he and Liang traded several messages, and he began plotting to revolt from Wei. Wei sent Sima Yi against him; Da was caught and killed at once. Liang never marched to his aid, for he knew Da lacked genuine loyalty. Under Jiang Wan's administration Shi was named remonstrance counsellor and ended his days in private life.
王沖者，廣漢人也。為牙門將，統屬江州李嚴。為嚴所疾，懼罪降魏。魏以沖為樂陵太守。〈孙盛蜀世谱曰：诗子立，晋散骑常侍。自后益州诸费有名位者，多是诗之后也。〉

Wang Chong came from Guanghan. He served as camp-gate general under Li Yan, the Jiangzhou commander. Yan hated him; dreading a reckoning, Chong fled to Wei. Wei made him prefect of Leling. Sun Sheng's Shu genealogy records that Shi's son Fei Li rose to supernumerary palace attendant and cavalier attendant-in-ordinary under the Jin. Most of the prominent Fei clansmen in Yi Province thereafter traced their line to Shi.
评曰：霍峻孤城不倾，王连固节不移，向朗好学不倦，张裔肤敏应机，杨洪乃心忠公，费诗率意而言，皆有可纪焉。以先主之广济，诸葛之准绳，诗吐直言，犹用陵迟，况庸后乎哉！

The historian concludes: Huo Jun held a single citadel unbroken; Wang Lian kept his integrity unbent; Xiang Lang never tired of study; Zhang Yi was alert and resourceful; Yang Hong gave his whole heart to the state; Fei Shi spoke his mind without flattery— each deserves to be remembered. Even under a ruler as magnanimous as the First Lord and a minister as exacting as Zhuge Liang, blunt counsel earned Fei Shi only demotion— what hope, then, for lesser lords who followed?
042: 杜微字國輔，梓潼涪人也。少受學於廣漢任安。劉障辟為從事，以疾去官。及先主定蜀，微常稱聾，閉門不出。

Du Wei, courtesy name Guofu, came from Fu in Zitong commandery. As a young man he studied under Ren An of Guanghan. Liu Zhang appointed him adjutant, but illness forced him to resign. After the First Lord conquered Shu, Wei feigned deafness and shut himself away.
建興二年，丞相亮領益州牧。選迎皆妙簡舊德，以秦宓為別駕，五梁為功曹，微為主簿。微固辭，舉而致之。既致，亮引見微，微自陳謝。亮以微不聞人語，於坐上與書曰：

In the second year of Jianxing, Chancellor Zhuge Liang added the title of shepherd of Yi Province. His appointments favored established worthies: Qin Mi became chief clerk on tour, Wu Liang merit assessor, and Du Wei chief secretary. Wei refused repeatedly until they virtually escorted him to office. Once there, Liang received him in audience; Wei apologized and begged off. Knowing Wei could not hear conversation, Liang wrote him a note at the table:
服聞德行，飢渴歷時，清濁異流，無緣諮覯。王元泰、李伯仁、王文儀、楊季休、丁君乾、李永南兄弟、文仲寶等，每歎高志，未見如舊。猥以空虛，統領貴州，德薄任重，慘慘憂慮、朝廷主公今年始十八，天姿仁敏，愛德下士。天下之人思慕漢室，欲與君因天順民，輔此明主，以隆季興之功，著勳於竹帛也。以謂賢愚下相為謀，故自割絕，守勞而已，不圖自屈也。

I have long admired your character, yet our paths never crossed— like clear and muddy waters that never mingle. Wang Yuantai, Li Borun, Wang Wenyi, Yang Jixiu, Ding Junqian, the Li Yongnan brothers, Wen Zhongbao, and the rest often spoke of your high aims and regretted losing touch. I govern this land with scant virtue and a crushing burden, anxious day and night. Our sovereign has only just turned eighteen— gifted, humane, and eager to honor men of talent. All under Heaven yearn for Han. I hope you will join me in aiding this enlightened ruler, Heaven and the people willing, to rebuild the dynasty's fortunes and win a place in history. I thought men of different gifts seldom counsel one another, so I kept my distance and minded my own office— I never meant to impose on you.
微自乞老病求歸，亮又與書答曰：
Du Wei pleaded age and infirmity and asked to retire. Liang wrote again:
曹丕篡弒，自立為帝，是猶土龍芻狗之有名也。欲與羣賢因其邪偽，以正道滅之。怪君未有相誨，便欲求還於山野。丕又大興勞役，以向吳、楚。今因丕多務，且以閉境勤農，育養民物，並治甲兵，以待其挫，然後伐之，可使兵不戰民不勞而天下定也。君但當以德輔時耳，不責君軍事，何為汲汲欲求去乎！

Cao Pi murdered his sovereign and stole the throne— a puppet emperor, as hollow as a clay dragon or a paper dog. I mean to join every able man in using his own treason to crush him with the righteous cause. I am surprised you offer no counsel yet already seek the hills and forests. Cao Pi has again launched vast levies against the southeast. While he is overstretched, we should seal the passes, encourage farming, rest the people, and forge arms until his strength flags— then strike so that armies need not clash and the realm may be pacified without exhausting the common folk. I ask only that you lend the age your moral weight, not that you bear arms— why this desperate hurry to withdraw?
其敬微如此，拜為諫議大夫，以從其志。五梁者，字德山，犍為南安人也，以儒學節操稱。從議郎遷諫義大夫、五官中朗將。

Such was Liang's deference: he named Wei remonstrance counsellor and let him live as he wished. Wu Liang of Nanan in Qianwei, courtesy name Deshan, was known for scholarship and moral fiber. He rose from master of discussion to remonstrance grandee and general of the household for the five offices.

周羣字仲直，巴西閬中人也。父舒，字叔布，少學術於廣漢楊厚，名亞董扶、任安。數被徵，終不詣。時人有問：「《春秋讖》曰『代漢者當塗高』，此何謂也？」舒曰：「當塗高者，魏也。」鄉黨學者私傳其語，羣少受學於舒，專心候業。於庭中做小樓，家富多奴，常令奴更直於樓上視天災，才見一氣，即白羣，羣自上樓觀之，不避晨夜，故凡有氣候，無不見之者，是以所言多中。州牧劉璋辟以為師友從事。〈《續漢書》曰：建安七年，越巂有男子化為女人，時羣言哀帝時亦有此，將易代之祥也。至二十五年，獻帝果封於山陽。十二年十月，有星孛於鶉尾，荊州分野，羣以為荊州牧將死而失土。明年秋，劉表卒，曹公平荊州。十七年十二月，星孛於五諸侯，羣以為西方專據土地者皆將失土。是時，劉璋據益州，張魯據漢中，韓遂據涼州，宋建據枹罕。明年冬，曹公遣偏將擊涼州。十九年，獲宋建，韓遂逃於羌中，被殺。其年秋，璋失益州。二十年秋，曹公攻漢中，張魯降。〉先主定蜀，署儒林校尉。

Zhou Qun, courtesy name Zhongzhi, came from Langzhong in Ba commandery. His father Zhou Shu, courtesy name Shubu, studied under Yang Hou of Guanghan in youth and stood just below Dong Fu and Ren An in reputation. Court summoned him repeatedly; he never answered. A contemporary once asked how to read the prophecy, "He who replaces Han shall be High on the Road." Zhou Shu answered, "High on the Road points to Wei." Scholars repeated his gloss in private. Zhou Qun studied under his father and devoted himself to celestial divination. He put up a small tower in the courtyard and set slaves to watch the sky in shifts day and night. The moment a portent appeared they roused Qun, who climbed to study it himself. Because he missed nothing, his forecasts usually came true. Liu Zhang, as shepherd, named him adjutant for teachers and friends. The Continued Han History records that in the seventh year of Jianan a man in Yuexi turned into a woman. Qun likened it to an omen from Emperor Ai's reign and called it a sign of dynastic change. By the twenty-fifth year of Jianan the abdicated emperor had indeed been enfeoffed at Shanyang. In the tenth month of the twelfth year of Jianan a comet swept the Quail's Tail asterism, Jing Province's celestial field. Qun predicted the death of Jing's shepherd and the loss of his territory. The following autumn Liu Biao died and Cao Cao took Jing Province. In the twelfth month of the seventeenth year a comet crossed the Five Feudatories. Qun read it as doom for every western warlord who clung to territory. Liu Zhang still held Yi, Zhang Lu Hanzhong, Han Sui Liangzhou, and Song Jian the Fuhan salient. The next winter Cao Cao sent a column against Liangzhou. In the nineteenth year Song Jian was taken; Han Sui fled to the Qiang and died there. That same autumn Liu Zhang lost Yi Province. In the autumn of the twentieth year Cao Cao invaded Hanzhong and Zhang Lu yielded. After the First Lord settled Shu he named Qun colonel of the forest of scholars.
先主欲曹公爭漢中，問羣，羣對曰：「當得其地，不得其民也，若出偏軍，必不利，當戒慎之！」時州後部司馬蜀郡張裕亦曉佔候，而天才過羣，〈裕字南和。〉諫先主曰：「不可爭漢中，軍必不利。」先主竟不用裕言，果得地而不得民也。遣將軍吳蘭、雷銅等入成都，皆沒不還，悉如羣言。於是舉羣茂才。

Planning to wrest Hanzhong from Cao Cao, the First Lord asked Qun's opinion. Qun said, "You will take the ground but not the population. A detached column will fare badly— proceed with utmost care." Zhang Yu of Shu, the province's rear army marshal, was an even keener astrologer than Qun, Zhang Yu's courtesy name was Nanhe. He warned the First Lord, "Do not contest Hanzhong— the expedition will end badly." The First Lord ignored Zhang Yu and, as predicted, won the terrain but not the people. He sent Wu Lan, Lei Tong, and others on the detached columns; they were swallowed up without return— exactly as Zhou Qun had foretold. Qun was then recommended as flourishing talent.

裕又私語人曰：「歲在庚子，天下當易代，劉氏祚盡矣。主公得益州，九年之後，寅卯之間當失之。」入密白其言。初，先主與劉璋會涪，時裕為璋從事，侍坐，其人饒須，先主嘲之曰：「昔吾居涿縣，特多毛姓，東西南北皆諸毛也，涿令稱曰『諸毛繞涿居乎』！」裕即答曰：「昔有作上黨潞長，遷為涿令者，去官還家，時人與書，欲署潞則失涿，欲署涿則失潞，乃署曰：『潞涿君』。先主無須，故裕以此及之。先主常銜莫不遜，加忿其漏言，乃顯裕諫爭漢中不驗，下獄，將誅之。諸葛亮表請其罪，先主答曰：「勞蘭生門，不得不鋤。」裕遂棄市。後魏氏之立，先主之薨，皆如裕所刻。又曉相術，每舉鏡視面，自知刑死，未常不撲之於地也。

Zhang Yu also whispered that in the gengzi year the mandate would turn and the house of Liu would be finished. Our lord had taken Yi Province; within nine years, between the yin and mao branches, he would lose it." An informer carried his words to the throne. Long ago, when the First Lord met Liu Zhang at Fu, Zhang Yu sat with Zhang's staff, heavily bearded. The First Lord teased him: "When I lived in Zhuo, every lane seemed full of Maos; the magistrate joked, The Maos wrap Zhuo on every side!" Yu shot back: "Once a man was magistrate of Lu in Shangdang and moved to Zhuo. Letters addressed to either place dropped the other title, so folk simply called him Lord Lu-Zhuo." The First Lord was beardless— Yu's barb hit its mark. The First Lord never forgave the slight, and Yu's loose talk sealed his fate: his failed warning about Hanzhong was trumped up as false prophecy and he was jailed for execution. Zhuge Liang pleaded for him, but the First Lord answered, "When weeds spring beside the orchid, you have to cut them down." Zhang Yu was executed in the marketplace. Later events— Wei's rise and the First Lord's death— unfolded on the schedule Zhang Yu had scratched out. He also read faces: every time he lifted a mirror he saw his own doom and always hurled it down.
羣卒，子臣頗傳其術。
After Qun died his son Zhou Chen inherited part of his craft.

杜瓊字伯瑜，蜀郡成都人也。少受學於任安，精究安術。劉璋時辟為從事，先主定益州，領牧，以瓊為議曹從事。後主踐阼，拜諫議大夫，遷左中郎將、大鴻臚、太常。為人靜默少言，闔門自守，不與世事。蔣琬、費禕等皆器重之。雖學業入深，初不視天文有所論說。後近通儒譙周常問其意，瓊答曰：「欲明此術甚難，須當身視，識其形色，不可信人也。晨夜苦劇，然後知之，復憂漏洩，不如不知，是以不復視也。」周因問曰：「昔周徵君以為當塗高者魏也，其義何也？」瓊答曰：「魏，闕名也，當塗而高，聖人取類而言耳。」又問周曰：「寧復有所怪邪？」周曰：「未達也。」瓊又曰：「古者名官職不言曹，始自漢已來，名官盡言曹。吏言屬曹，卒言侍曹，此殆天意也。」

Du Qiong, courtesy name Boyu, was a native of Chengdu in Shu commandery. He studied under Ren An in youth and mastered Ren's methods. Liu Zhang had appointed him adjutant; after the First Lord took Yi Province and the shepherd's seal, he made Qiong adjutant of the deliberation bureau. Under the Later Lord he rose from remonstrance grandee to general of the left in the palace, grand herald, and grand master of ceremonies. He was a man of few words who kept his doors shut and held aloof from public life. Jiang Wan, Fei Yi, and their circle held him in high regard. For all his learning he rarely lectured on astrology. Later Qiao Zhou pressed him on the subject. Qiong replied, "That art is hard to teach: you must watch the sky yourself and learn the shapes— you cannot take another's word." It means sleepless nights of observation, and even then you dread letting secrets slip— ignorance may be safer, so I no longer watch the heavens." Zhou pressed him: "Your father read High on the Road as Wei— what did he mean?" Qiong said, "Wei names the palace gate; standing high on the road— the sage was speaking in riddles." Zhou asked again whether anything else seemed odd. Zhou admitted he still did not see it. Qiong added, "Ancient offices were not called cao; since Han every bureau is a cao. Officials speak of their cao, soldiers of attending cao— that may be Heaven's own pun on the house of Cao."
瓊年八十餘，延熙十三年卒。著《韓詩章句》十餘萬言，不教諸子，內學無傳業者。周緣瓊言，乃觸類而長之曰：

He died in the thirteenth year of Yanxi, aged over eighty. He wrote over ten thousand characters of commentary on the Han version of the Odes but taught none of his sons; his esoteric learning died with him. Taking his cue from Du Qiong, Qiao Zhou pressed the same logic further:
《春秋傳》著秦穆候名太子曰仇，弟曰成師。師服曰：『異哉君之名子也！嘉耦曰妃，怨耦曰仇，今君名太子曰仇，弟曰成師，始兆亂矣，兄其替乎？』其後果如服言。及漢靈帝名二子曰史候、董候，既立為帝，後皆免為諸侯，與師服言相似也。先主諱備，其訓具也，後主諱禪，其訓授也，如言劉已具矣，當授與人也；意者甚於穆候、靈帝之名子。

The Zuo tradition tells how Duke Mu of Qin named his heir Chou and his younger son Chengshi. Shi Fu exclaimed, "What strange names the duke has chosen for his sons!" A loving match is fei; a hostile match is chou. To call the heir Chou and the younger brother Chengshi is to invite strife— will the elder lose his place?" Events proved Shi Fu right. Emperor Ling named two sons Marquis of Shi and Marquis of Dong; both briefly mounted the throne and were then reduced to common nobles— another echo of Shi Fu's warning. The First Lord's name Bei means "complete"; the Later Lord's name Shan means "to yield"— as if the house of Liu were finished and ready to pass the mandate on; a darker omen than Duke Mu's or Lingdi's choice of names.
後宦人黃皓弄權於內，景耀五年，宮中大樹無故自折，周深憂之，無所與言，乃書柱曰：「眾而大，期之會，具而授，若何復？」言曹者眾也，魏者大也，眾而大，天下其當會也，具而授，如何復有立者乎？蜀既亡，咸以周言為驗。周曰：「此雖己所推尋，然有所因，由杜君之辭而廣之耳，殊無神思獨至之異也。」

Later, as Huang Hao meddled at court, a great tree in the palace snapped without wind in the fifth year of Jingyao. Zhou scratched a couplet on a pillar: "Many and great— the hour draws near; complete then yielded— what can rise again?" Cao means "host of officials"; wei means "great." Many and great— the realm will unite under Wei. Complete and yielded— how could Shu stand again?" After Shu fell, everyone called Zhou a prophet. Qiao Zhou said, "I only extended what Du Qiong had already hinted; there was no mystic flash of my own."

許慈字仁篤，南陽人也。師事劉熙，善鄭氏學，治《易》、《尚書》、《三禮》、《毛詩》、《論語》。建安中，與許靖等俱自交州入蜀。時又有魏郡胡潛，字公興，不知其所以在益土。潛雖學不沾洽，然卓犖強識，祖宗制度之儀，喪紀五服之數，皆指掌畫地，舉手可採。先主定蜀，承喪亂歷紀，學業衰廢，乃鳩合典籍，沙汰眾學。慈、潛並為學士，與孟光、來敏等典掌舊文。值庶事草創，動多疑議，慈、潛更相剋伐，謗讟忿急，形於聲色；書籍有無，不相通借，時尋楚撻，以相震攇。〈攇，虛晚反。〉其矜己妒彼，乃至於此。先主愍其若斯，羣僚大會，使倡家假為二子之容，效其訟鬩之狀，酒酣樂作，以為嬉戲。初以辭義相難，終以刀杖相屈，用感切之。潛先沒，慈後主世稍遷至大長秋，卒。〈孫盛曰：蜀少人士，故慈、潛等並見載述。〉子勳傳其業，復為博士。

Xu Ci, courtesy name Rendu, came from Nanyang. He studied under Liu Xi, mastered the Zheng school tradition, and worked through the Changes, Documents, the three ritual texts, Mao's Poetry, and the Analects. During the Jianan years he crossed from Jiaozhou into Shu with Xu Jing and others. Hu Qian of Wei commandery, courtesy name Gongxing, had also turned up in Shu for reasons now unknown. Qian's scholarship was patchy, but his memory was prodigious: ancestral temple protocol, mourning grades, and five-garment rules— he could trace them in the dust from memory. After the First Lord conquered Shu, years of war had ruined scholarship; he gathered texts and culled the scholars. Xu Ci and Hu Qian became court erudites alongside Meng Guang and Lai Min, charged with curating the classics. In those rough early days every policy sparked quarrels; Ci and Qian sniped at each other with public insults and black looks; they hoarded books from each other and sometimes squared off with rods, trying to intimidate one another. The character xian is glossed with the reading xu-wan. Their vanity and mutual jealousy had sunk to such depths. The First Lord took pity on their feud. At a full court banquet he had actors mimic the two scholars, acting out their bickering for comic relief once the wine flowed. The skit began with verbal sparring and ended in a mock brawl with props— a pointed lesson in how ugly their rivalry had become. Hu Qian died first. Xu Ci survived into the Later Lord's reign, rose to grand prolonger of autumn, and died there. Sun Sheng notes that Shu produced few famous scholars, which is why Xu Ci and Hu Qian earned a place in the record. His son Xu Xun inherited his scholarship and again held the title of court erudite.
孟光字孝裕，河南洛陽人，漢太尉孟鬱之族。〈《續漢書》曰：鬱，中常侍孟賁之弟。〉靈帝末為講部吏。獻帝遷都長安，遂逃人蜀，劉焉父子待以客禮。博物識古，無書不覽，尤銳意三史，長於漢家舊典。好《公羊春秋》而譏呵《左氏》，每與來敏爭此二義，光常譊譊讙咋。〈譊音奴交反。讙音休袁反。咋音徂格反。〉先主定益州，拜為儀郎，與許慈等並掌制度。後主踐阼，為符節令、屯騎校尉、長樂少府，遷大司農。

Meng Guang, courtesy name Xiaoyu, came from Luoyang in Henan and belonged to the line of Han grand commandant Meng Yu. The Continued Han History identifies Meng Yu as the younger brother of the eunuch Meng Ben. Under Emperor Ling he served as a clerk in the lecture bureau. When the emperor moved the court west to Chang'an, Guang fled into Shu, where Liu Yan and Liu Zhang received him as an honored guest. He was encyclopedic, read everything, and took special interest in the three histories and Han institutional precedent. He favored the Gongyang commentary and scorned the Zuo; with Lai Min he argued the point endlessly, shouting himself hoarse. The character nao is glossed nu-jiao. The character huan is glossed xiu-yuan. The character zha is glossed zu-ge. After the First Lord took Yi Province he named Guang master of ceremonies alongside Xu Ci to codify court ritual. Under the Later Lord he rose from marshal of credentials and colonel of the agile cavalry to junior steward of Changle palace and finally grand minister of agriculture.

延熙九年秋，大赦，光於眾中責大將軍費禕曰：「夫赦者，偏枯之物，非明世所宜有也。衰弊窮極，必不得已，然後乃可權而行之耳。今主上仁賢，百僚稱職，有何旦夕之危，倒懸之急，而數施非常之恩，以惠姦宄之惡乎？又鷹隼始擊，而更原宥有罪，上犯天時，下違人理。老夫耄朽，不達治體，窮謂其法難以經久，豈具瞻之高美，所望於明德哉。」禕但顧謝踧踖而已。光之指摘痛癢，多如是類。故執政重臣，心不能悅，爵位不登，每直言無所迴避，為代所嫌。太常廣漢鐔承、〈《華陽國志》曰：承字公文，歷郡守少府。〉光祿勛河東裴儁等，年資皆在光後，而登據上列，處光之右，蓋以此也。〈傅暢《裴氏家記》曰：儁字奉先，魏尚書令潛弟也。儁姊夫爲蜀中長史，儁送之，時年十餘歲，遂遭漢末大亂，不復得還。既長知名，爲蜀所推重也。子越，字令緒，爲蜀督軍。蜀破，遷還洛陽，拜議郎。〉

When a general amnesty was proclaimed in the ninth year of Yanxi, Guang publicly scolded Fei Yi: "Mercy decrees are a crutch for failing states, not the tool of a well-ordered realm. They belong to ages of collapse, when there is truly no alternative— only then may you resort to them." Our sovereign is wise, his ministers capable— what sudden peril warrants showering criminals with repeated pardons?" Autumn is the season of the law, yet you spare felons— you offend both the calendar and common sense." I am an old fool out of touch with policy, yet I know this habit cannot last— is this what the world expects of enlightened rule?" Fei Yi could only bow and mumble apologies, squirming in his seat. Guang's blunt rebukes were typical of his manner. The great officers of state resented him, he rose no higher in rank, and his habit of blunt truth-telling made him widely disliked. Tan Cheng of Guanghan, grand master of ceremonies, the Huayang Guo zhi gives his courtesy name as Gongwen and lists him as a former commandery governor and junior steward. Minister of the household Pei Jun of Hedong and others were junior to Guang in age and service yet ranked above him— largely because Guang had alienated the powerful. Fu Chang's Pei family record identifies Jun as courtesy Fengxian, younger brother of Wei director Pei Qian. Jun had escorted a brother-in-law serving as chief clerk in Shu while still a boy; the wars stranded him there. He grew up in Shu, won a reputation, and became a respected figure. His son Pei Yue, courtesy Lingxu, became an army supervisor in Shu. After Shu fell he returned to Luoyang as a master of discussion.

後進文士秘書郎郤正數從光諮訪，光問正太子所習讀性並其性情好尚，正答曰：「奉親虔恭。夙夜匪懈，有古世子之風；接待羣僚，舉動出於仁恕。」光曰：「如君所道，皆家戶所有耳；吾今所問，欲知其權略智調何如也。」正曰：「世子之道，在於承志竭歡，既不得妄有所施為，且智調藏於胸懷，權略應時而發，此之有無，焉可豫設也？」光解正慎宜，不為放談，乃曰：「吾好直言，無所迴避，每彈射利病，為世人所譏嫌。疑省君意亦不甚好吾言，然語有次。今天下未定，智意為先，智意雖有自然，然不可力強致也。此儲君讀書，寧當效吾等竭力博識以待訪問，如博士探策講試以求爵位邪！當務其急者。」正深謂光言為然。後光坐事免官，年九十餘，卒。

The young secretary Xi Zheng often sought Guang's counsel. Guang asked what the heir read and what sort of man he was. Zheng answered, "He honors his parents with devotion. He is diligent night and day in the mold of the classical heir; and in dealing with officials he acts from benevolence and forbearance." Guang replied, "That is the sort of praise any family could mouth; I want to know his strategic mind and practical judgment." Zheng said, "An heir's duty is to please his father and carry on his will; he cannot scheme in the open. Clever plans stay hidden until the moment calls for them— you cannot know that in advance." Guang saw that Zheng was being discreet and said, "I always speak plainly and pay for it with the world's dislike. I suspect you do not much like my tone either, yet there is a point to my order of topics. The empire is still unsettled; judgment matters most, and judgment cannot be forced. Should the heir exhaust himself cramming trivia like a student cramming for an exam to win a salary?" He should master what is urgent." Zheng agreed wholeheartedly. Guang later lost his post over an incident and died in his nineties.

來敏字敬達，義陽新野人，來歙之後也。父艷，為漢司空。〈華嶠《後漢書》曰：艷好學下士，開館養徒眾。少歷顯位，靈帝時位至司空。〉漢末大亂，敏隨姊夫奔荊州，姊夫黃琬是劉璋祖母之侄，故璋遣迎琬妻，敏遂俱與姊入蜀，常為璋賓客。涉獵書籍，善《左氏春秋》，尤精於《倉》、《雅》訓詁，好是正文字。先主定益州，署敏典學校尉。及立太子，以為家令。後主踐阼，為虎賁中郎將。丞相亮住漢中，請為軍祭酒、輔軍將軍，坐事去職。〈亮集有教曰：「將軍來敏對上官顯言『新人有何功德而奪我榮資與之邪？諸人共憎我，何故如是』？敏年老狂悖，生此怨言。昔成都初定，議者以為來敏亂羣，先帝以新定之際，故遂含容，無所禮用。後劉子初選以為太子家令，先帝不悅而不忍拒也。後主既位，吾闇於知人，遂復擢為將軍祭酒，違議者之審見，背先帝所疏外，自謂能以敦厲薄俗，帥之以義。今既不能，表退職，使閉門思愆。」〉亮卒後，還成都為大長秋，又免，後累遷為光祿大夫，復坐過黜。前後數貶削，皆以語言不節，舉動違常也。時孟光亦以樞機不慎，議論干時，然猶愈於敏，俱以耆宿學士見禮於世。而敏荊楚名族，東宮舊臣，特加優待，是故廢而復起。後以敏為執慎將軍，欲令以官重自警戒也，年九十七，景耀中卒。子忠，亦博覽經學，有敏風，與尚書向充等並能協贊大將軍姜維。維善之，以為參軍。

Lai Min, courtesy name Jingda, from Xinye in Yiyang, descended from Lai Xi. His father Lai Yan had been Han minister of works. Hua Qiao's Later Han History says Lai Yan loved books, honored scholars, and kept a school full of pupils. He rose early to high office and became minister of works under Emperor Ling. When the Han collapsed, Min fled to Jing with his brother-in-law Huang Wan, a kinsman of Liu Zhang's grandmother. Liu Zhang summoned Wan's household west, so Min entered Shu with his sister and stayed on as Liu Zhang's client. He read widely, excelled in the Zuo commentary, and specialized in the Cangjie and Erya wordbooks, loving to emend textual errors. The First Lord named him colonel of classical schools after taking Yi Province. When the heir apparent was named, Min became his household steward. Under the Later Lord he was promoted to general of the tiger garrison at the center. Zhuge Liang, stationed at Hanzhong, made him army libationer and general who assists the army, but he later lost the post over an incident. Among Zhuge Liang's papers is an order noting that General Lai Min had loudly demanded of his superiors, "What have these newcomers done to strip me of my honors and pay?" Everyone turns on me— why should it be so?" Min is old, unbalanced, and mutinous." When Chengdu first fell, many had called Min a disruptive influence; the First Lord had only tolerated him while the realm was new. Later Liu Ba proposed him as the heir's steward; the First Lord disliked the choice but let it stand. When I took the throne I misjudged him and raised him again as libationer to the general— against good advice and contrary to my father's coldness toward him— thinking I could shame him into reform. Since he will not mend his ways, strip his office and make him reflect behind closed doors." After Liang's death he came back to Chengdu as grand prolonger of autumn, lost that post, later rose to grand counselor of the household, and was demoted again for misconduct. Each fall was for loose talk and erratic behavior. Meng Guang likewise offended the court with ill-timed opinions, though he was still easier to bear than Min; both were honored as senior scholars. Yet Min belonged to a great Jing-Chu lineage and had long served the heir's household, so the court kept restoring him after each dismissal. He was eventually named general who holds caution in hope that the title would sober him; he died in the Jingyao era at ninety-seven. His son Lai Zhong inherited his breadth of learning and, with Xiang Chong of the Masters of Writing, helped Jiang Wei as grand general. Wei valued him and named him an army adviser.

尹默字思潛，梓潼涪人也。益部多貴今文而不祟章句，默知其不博。乃遠遊荊州，從司馬德操、宋仲子等受古學。皆通諸經史，又專精於《左氏春秋》，自劉歆條例，鄭眾、賈逵父子、陳元、方服虔注說，咸略誦述，不復按本。先主定益州，領牧，以為勸學從事。及立太子，以默為僕，射以《左氏傳》授後主。後主踐阼，拜諫議大夫。丞相亮住漢中，請為軍祭酒。亮卒，還成都，拜大中大夫，卒。子宗傳其業，為博士。〈宋仲子後在魏。《魏略》曰：其子與魏諷謀反，伏誅。魏太子答王朗書曰：「昔石厚與州吁遊，父碏知其與亂；韓子暱田蘇，穆子知其好仁：故君子遊必有方，居必就士，誠有以也。嗟乎！宋忠無石子先識之明，老罹此禍。今雖欲原行滅親之誅，立純臣之節，尚可得邪！」〉

Yin Mo, courtesy name Sizian, came from Fu in Zitong. Yi scholars favored modern-text studies and scorned philology; Mo saw how narrow that was. He went to Jing Province to study antiquity under Sima Hui, Song Zhongzi, and others. He mastered the classics and histories and made the Zuo commentary his specialty, committing Liu Xin's outlines and the glosses of Zheng Zhong, the Jias, Chen Yuan, Fang, and Fu Qian to memory without needing the text. After the First Lord took Yi Province and the shepherd's seal, he appointed Mo adjutant for encouraging learning. When the heir apparent was installed, Mo became his tutor and taught the Later Lord from the Zuo Tradition. The Later Lord named him remonstrance grandee at accession. While Zhuge Liang was at Hanzhong he summoned Mo as army libationer. After Liang's death he returned to Chengdu as grand palace counselor and died there. His son Yin Zong inherited his learning and became a court erudite. Song Zhongzi later ended up in Wei. The Wei lüe records that Zhongzi's son joined Wei Feng's plot and was put to death. The Wei crown prince once wrote Wang Lang: "Shi Hou kept company with Zhou Xu, and his father knew it meant trouble; Hanzi befriended Tian Su, and Viscount Mu saw his goodness— a gentleman chooses his company with care for good reason. Alas! Song Zhong lacked Shi Que's foresight and paid for it in old age. Even if one wished to execute a son to prove a father's loyalty, that purity is beyond reach now!"
譙周字允南，巴西西充國人也。父（山幷），字榮始，治《尚書》，兼通諸經及圖緯。州郡辟請，皆不應，州就假師友從事。周幼孤，與母兄同居。既長，耽古篤學，家貧未嘗問產業，誦讀典籍，欣然獨笑，以忘寢食。研精《六經》，尤善書札，頗曉天文，而不以留意；諸子文章非心所存，不悉遍視也。身長八尺，體貌素樸，性推誠不飾。無造次辯論之才，然潛識內敏。

Qiao Zhou, courtesy name Yunnan, came from Xichongguo in Ba commandery. His father (the manuscript preserves a garbled form of his father's name) , courtesy name Rongshi, specialized in the Documents and the esoteric classics and apocrypha. He refused every provincial summons until the authorities named him acting adjutant for teachers and friends without his consent. Zhou lost his father young and lived with his mother and older brother. Grown to manhood he buried himself in the classics, indifferent to poverty, chuckling over his books until he forgot meals and sleep. He absorbed the Six Classics, wrote elegant prose, and knew something of astronomy though he cared little for it; and he skimmed the philosophers only when he had to. He stood eight chi tall, dressed plainly, and was candid to a fault. He was no quick debater but saw to the heart of things.
建興中，丞相亮領益州牧，命周為勸學從事。〈《蜀記》曰：周初見亮，左右皆笑。既出，有司請推笑者，亮曰：「孤尚不能忍，況左右乎！」〉亮卒於敵庭，周在家聞問，即便奔赴，尋有詔書禁斷，惟周以速行得達。大將軍蔣琬領刺史，徙為典學從事，總州之學者。後主立太子，以周為僕，轉家令。時後主頗出遊觀，增廣聲樂。周上疏諫曰：

During Jianxing, while Zhuge Liang held stewardship of Yi Province, he named Zhou adjutant for encouraging learning. The Shu ji notes that when Qiao Zhou first met Zhuge Liang, the attendants laughed at him. Afterward officials wanted to punish the snickerers. Liang said, "If I could barely keep a straight face, how can I blame the staff?" When Liang died on campaign, Zhou set out from home at once. An edict soon forbade travel for mourning, but Zhou moved so fast he arrived before the ban caught him. Grand general Jiang Wan, as concurrent provincial inspector, moved him to adjutant for canonical learning to oversee the province's scholars. When the heir apparent was installed, Zhou became his tutor and then his household steward. The Later Lord had begun touring the parks and expanding his musical establishments. Zhou therefore memorialized:

昔王莽之敗，豪傑並起，跨州據郡，欲弄神器，於是賢才智士思望所歸，未必以其勢之廣狹，惟其德之薄厚也。是故於時更始、公孫述及諸有大眾者多己廣大，然莫不快情恣欲，怠於為善，遊獵飲食，不恤民物。世祖初入河北，馮異等勸之曰：『當行人所不能為。』遂務理冤獄，節儉飲食，動尊法度，故北州歌歎，聲布四遠。於是鄧禹自南陽追之，吳漢、寇恂未識世祖，遙聞德行，遂以權計舉漁陽、上谷突騎迎於廣阿。其望風慕德者邳肜、耿純、劉植之徒，至於輿病繼棺，繈負而至者，不可勝數，故能以弱為強，屠王郎，吞銅馬，折赤眉而成帝業也。及在洛陽，嘗欲小出，車駕已御，銚期諫曰：『天下未寧，臣誠不願陛下細行數出。』即時還車。及征隗囂，穎川盜起，世祖還洛陽，但遣寇恂往，恂曰：『穎川以陛下遠征，故奸猾起叛，未知陛下還，恐不時降；陛下自臨，穎川賊必即降。』遂至穎川，竟如恂言。故非急務，欲小出不敢，至於急務，欲自安不為，故帝者之欲善也如此！故《傳》曰『百姓不徒附』，誠以德先之也。今漢遭厄運，天下三分，雄哲之士思望之時也。陛下天姿至孝，喪逾三年，言及隕涕，雖曾、閔不過也。敬賢任才，使之盡力，有逾成、康。故國內和一，大小戮力，臣所不能陳。然臣不勝大願，願復廣人所不能者。夫挽大重者，其用力苦不眾，拔大艱者，其善術苦不廣，且承事宗廟者，非徒求福祐，所以率民尊上也。至於四時之祀，或有不臨，池苑之觀；或有仍出，臣之愚滯，私不自安。夫憂責在身者，不暇盡樂，先帝之志，堂構未成，誠非盡樂之時。願省減樂官、後宮所增造，但奉備先帝所施，下為子孫節儉之教。

When Wang Mang fell, warlords carved up the realm. Wise men chose their lords by moral weight, not by the size of an army. Gengshi, Gongsun Shu, and other large factions grew arrogant: they hunted, feasted, and ignored the people. When Guangwu first entered Hebei, Feng Yi urged him to do what others would not— win the people by justice. He cleared wrongful convictions, lived simply, and honored the law until the north sang his praises. Deng Yu rode from Nanyang to join him; Wu Han and Kou Xun, though they had never met him, sent the crack cavalry of Fuyang and Shanggu to meet him at Guang'e on the strength of his reputation. Men such as Pi Tong and Geng Chun flocked to him— some carried on sickbeds, others brought infants— too many to count. Thus he turned weakness into strength, destroyed Wang Lang, absorbed the Bronze Horse bands, crushed the Red Eyebrows, and founded the Eastern Han. Even at Luoyang, when he once ordered a minor outing, Yao Qi warned him, "The realm is still unsettled; please do not ride out on whim." He turned the chariot back at once. During the Wei Ao campaign, Yingchuan rebelled. Guangwu stayed in Luoyang and sent only Kou Xun, who said, "The rebels think you are still far away; they will not yield until they know you have returned; but if you appear in person, they will collapse at once." He rode south and it happened exactly as Kou Xun predicted. He would not stir for pleasure, yet never shirked duty— such was an emperor's discipline. The classic line runs, "The people do not rally without reason"— they follow virtue first. Han is broken into three; this is the hour when heroes choose their lord. Your filial mourning for the late emperor exceeded three years and moved all who heard you— Zengzi and Min Sun could have done no more. You honor the worthy and employ talent to the full— a standard beyond even the kings Cheng and Kang. The realm is united and every rank pulls together— more than words can say. Yet I beg you to attempt what common men find hardest. Great burdens need many hands; grave crises need broad counsel. Tending the shrines is not mere ritual— it teaches the people to revere their ruler. Yet seasonal rites are sometimes missed for pleasure trips to pools and parks; and the court still rides out for sport— this dull subject cannot rest easy. A man with the weight of the realm on his shoulders cannot indulge every whim. Your father's work is unfinished— this is no season for revelry. Cut the music bureau and harem expansions, keep only what the late emperor ordained, and leave your heirs an example of thrift.
徙為中散大夫，猶侍太子。
He was shifted to grand master of scattered rank while remaining tutor to the heir.
於時軍旅數出，百姓凋瘁，周與尚書令陳祗論其利害，退而書之，謂之《仇國論》，其辭曰：
Constant campaigning had exhausted the people. Zhou debated policy with Chen Zhi, director of the Masters of Writing, then wrote the Discourse on Enemy States. It begins:

因餘之國小，而肇建之國大，並爭於世而為仇敵。因餘之國有高賢卿者，問於伏愚子曰：「今國事未定，上下勞心，往古之事，能以弱勝強者，其術何如？」伏愚子曰：「吾聞之，處大無患者恆多慢，處小有憂者恆思善；多慢則生亂，恩善則生治，理之常也。故周文養民，以少取多；勾踐卹眾，以弱斃強，此其術也。」賢卿曰：「囊者項強漢弱，相與戰爭，無日寧息，然項羽與漢約分鴻溝為界，各欲歸息民；張良以為民志既定，則難動也，尋帥追羽，終斃項氏，豈必由文王之事乎？肇建之國方有疾疢，我因其隙，陷其邊陲，覬增其疾而斃之也。」伏愚子曰：「當殷、周之際，王候世尊，君臣久固，民習所專；深根者難拔，據固者難遷。當此之時，雖漢祖安能杖劍鞭馬而取天下乎？當秦罷候置守之後，民疲秦役，天下土崩；或歲改主，或月易公，鳥驚獸駭，莫知所從，於是豪強並爭，虎裂狼分，疾搏者獲多，遲後者見吞。今我與肇建皆傳國易世矣，既非秦末鼎沸之時，實有六國並據之勢，故可為文王，難為漢祖。夫民疲勞，則騷擾之兆生，上慢下暴則瓦解之形起。諺曰：『射幸數跌，不如審發。』是故智者不為小利移目，不為意似改步，時可而後動，數合而後舉，故湯、武之師不再戰而克，誠重民勞而度時審也。如遂極武黜征，土崩勢生，不幸遇難，雖有智者將不能謀之矣；若乃奇變縱橫，出入無間，沖波截轍，超谷越山，不由舟楫而濟盟津者，我愚子也，實所不及。」

Imagine a small survivor state and a large new power locked in rivalry. A worthy minister of the lesser state asks a recluse: "In unstable times, how did the weak ever defeat the strong?" The recluse answers: "Great powers grow careless; small ones stay vigilant; carelessness breeds chaos, vigilance order— that is the rule of things." King Wen nourished his people and won many with few; Goujian cherished his troops and destroyed a stronger foe— that is the art." The minister objects: "Xiang Yu was strong, Han weak, yet they agreed at the Hong Canal to rest their peoples; but Zhang Liang argued that popular sentiment, once fixed, could not be stirred again; he drove the pursuit that finished Xiang Yu— need that imitate King Wen's slow virtue?" The new state is already ill; strike its borders and widen the crack until it dies." The recluse replies: "At the Yin-Zhou transition lords had ruled for generations; customs were fixed; deep roots resist uprooting and strongholds do not shift easily." In such an age not even Han Gaozu could have seized the realm by sword alone." After Qin replaced feudal lords with magistrates, the people collapsed under corvee; lords changed yearly, magistrates monthly; the realm panicked; strongmen tore it apart and the bold devoured the slow. Today we and Wei are both mature states, not the boiling chaos of Qin's end nor a simple duel of two powers— we may still play King Wen's patient game, but we cannot replay Han Gaozu's gambit." When the people tire, rebellion stirs; when rulers grow arrogant and subjects harsh, the state cracks. The proverb says, "Many hasty shots miss; one careful arrow hits." The wise ignore small bait and false openings; they strike when heaven and numbers align— hence Tang and Wu won without repeated battles, because they weighed the people's strength and the season." If you wage total war heedlessly, the realm crumbles; when disaster strikes, no wit can save you; and if you expect miracles— secret marches over mountains without fleets crossing the Yellow River— I am too dull for such schemes."
後遷光祿大夫，位亞九列。周雖不與政事，以儒行見禮。時訪大議，輒據經以對，而後生好事者亦諮問所疑焉。

He was later promoted to grand counselor of the household, just below the nine ministers. Though he held no executive power, the court honored him as a Confucian elder. Whenever great policy was debated, he answered from the classics, and younger scholars brought him their questions.
景耀六年冬，魏大將軍鄧艾克江由，長驅而前。而蜀本謂敵不便至，不作城守調度。及聞艾已人陰平，百姓擾擾，皆進山野，不可禁制。後主使臣羣會議，計無所出。或以為蜀之與吳，本為和國，宜可奔吳；或以為南中七郡，阻險鬥絕，易以自守，宜可奔南。惟周以為：

In the winter of Jingyao 6, Wei's Deng Ai broke through Jiangyou and raced inward. Shu had assumed the foe would not penetrate so fast and had left the passes undefended. When word spread that Deng Ai had crossed into Yinping, the populace panicked and fled to the hills beyond control. The Later Lord convened his ministers; no one had a plan. Some urged flight to Wu as a fellow state against Wei; others argued for the seven southern commanderies, rugged and remote, as a defensible refuge. Only Qiao Zhou argued that,
自古以來，無寄他國為天子者也，今若入吳，固當臣服。且政理不殊，則大能吞小，此數之自然也。由此言之，則魏能並吳，吳不能並魏明矣。等為小稱臣，孰與為大？再辱之恥，何與一辱？且若欲奔南，則當早為之計，然後可果；今大敵以近，禍敗將及，羣小之心，無一可保，恐發足之日，其變不測，何至南之有乎！

no Son of Heaven has ever ruled from a neighbor's court; if we flee to Wu we must bow to Sun Wu. Where institutions are alike, the larger power devours the smaller— that is arithmetic. Therefore Wei can absorb Wu, but Wu can never absorb Wei. Better to yield once to the greater power than twice to the lesser. Why suffer the double humiliation of vassalage to Wu and then to Wei? Flight south needed long preparation to succeed; now the enemy is at the gate and small men are unreliable— the moment you march south mutiny may break out. Why bother with the south at all?"
羣臣或難周曰：「今艾以不遠，恐不受降，如之何？」周曰：「方今東吳未賓，事勢不得不受之，受之後，不得不禮。若陛下降魏，魏不裂土以封陛下者，周請身詣京都，以古義爭之。」眾人無以易周之理。

Some objected: "Deng Ai is close; will he even accept our surrender?" Zhou answered, "Wu is still independent, so Wei must take our surrender to win prestige; having taken it, they must treat us with face. If Your Majesty yields to Wei and they refuse you a fief, I will go to Luoyang myself and argue from the classics for your due." No one could refute him.
後主猶疑於入南，周上疏曰：
The sovereign still wavered toward the south, so Zhou wrote again:

或說陛下以北兵深入，有欲適南之計，臣愚以為不安。何者？南方遠夷之地，平常無所供為，猶數反叛，自丞相亮南征，兵勢逼之，窮乃幸從，是後供出官賦，取以給兵，以為愁怨，此患國之人也。今以窮迫，欲往依恃，恐必復反叛，一也；北兵之來，非但取蜀而已，若奔南方，必因人勢衰，及時赴追，二也；若至南方，外當拒敵，內供服御，費用張廣，他無所取，耗損諸夷必甚，甚必速叛，三也；昔王郎以邯鄲僭號，時世祖在信都，畏逼於郎，欲棄還關中。邳肜諫曰：『明公西還，則邯鄲城民不肯捐父母，背城主，而千里送公，其亡叛可必也。』世祖從之，遂破邯鄲。今北兵至，陛下南行，誠恐邳肜之言覆信於今，四也。願陛下早為之圖，可獲爵土；若遂適南，勢窮乃服，其禍必深。《易》曰：『亢之為言，知而不知喪，知存而不知亡；知得失存亡而不失其正者，其惟聖人乎！」言聖人知命而不苟必也，故堯，舜以子不善，知天有授，而求授人；子雖不肖，禍尚未萌，而迎綬於人，況禍以至乎！故微子以殷王之昆，面縛銜璧而歸武王，豈所樂哉，不得已也。

Some say the northern advance makes the south the only refuge; I believe that path is perilous. Why? The south is wild country that even in peace pays little tax and often revolts. Zhuge Liang's expedition forced it to obey, and ever since it has groaned under levies for our armies— those peoples nurse a grudge against Shu. First, they will likely rebel if we lean on them in crisis; second, Wei did not march only against us; if we flee south they will follow our weakness and overtake us; third, a southern court would face Wei abroad and feed our court at home until the tribes broke under the strain and revolted; fourth, when Wang Lang seized Handan, Guangwu in Xindu nearly fled to Guanzhong; Pi Tong warned that a western retreat would make the people of Handan abandon their lord— sure mutiny. Guangwu listened and broke Wang Lang. If you run south today, Pi Tong's warning will come true again— that is my fourth point. Yield now and you may still win a title and lands; delay until ruin forces surrender and your fate will be far worse. The Book of Changes says of the top line, "Proud height means knowing gain but not loss, life but not death; knowing both fortune and ruin yet holding the mean— that is the sage alone." Sages accept heaven's mandate: Yao and Shun, seeing unworthy sons, sought worthier heirs; they yielded before disaster struck— how much more should we when disaster is at the door!" Weizi bound himself and offered the jade to King Wu of Zhou not from joy but from necessity.

於是遂從周策。劉氏無虞，一邦蒙賴，周之謀也。〈孫綽評曰：譙周說後主降魏，可乎？曰：自為天子而乞降請命，何恥之深乎！夫為社稷死則死之，為社稷亡則亡之。先君正魏之篡，不與同天矣。推過於其父，俛首而事讎，可謂苟存，豈大居正之道哉！孫盛曰：春秋之義，國君死社稷，卿大夫死位，況稱天子而可辱於人乎！周謂萬乘之君偷生苟免，亡禮希利，要冀微榮，惑矣。且以事勢言之，理有未盡。何者？禪雖庸主，實無桀、紂之酷，戰雖屢北，未有土崩之亂，縱不能君臣固守，背城借一，自可退次東鄙以思後圖。是時羅憲以重兵據白帝，霍弋以強卒鎮夜郎。蜀土險狹，山水峻隔，絕巘激湍，非步卒所涉。若悉取舟楫，保據江州，徵兵南中，乞師東國，如此則姜、廖五將自然雲從，吳之三師承命電赴，何投寄之無所而慮於必亡邪？魏師之來，褰國大舉，欲追則舟楫靡資，欲留則師老多虞。且屈伸有會，情勢代起，徐因思奮之民，以攻驕惰之卒，此越王所以敗闔閭，田單所以摧騎劫也，何為匆匆遽自囚虜，下堅壁於敵人，致斫石之至恨哉？葛生有云：「事之不濟則已耳，安能復為之下！」壯哉斯言，可以立懦夫之志矣。觀古燕、齊、荊、越之敗，或國覆主滅，或魚縣鳥竄，終能建功立事，康復社稷，豈曰天助，抑亦人謀也。向使懷苟存之計，納譙周之言，何邦基之能構，令名之可獲哉？禪既闇主，周實駑臣，方之申包、田單、范蠡、大夫種，不亦遠乎！〉

The court adopted Qiao Zhou's counsel. The Liu clan survived unharmed and the state was spared— thanks to Zhou's plan. Sun Chuo asks whether Qiao Zhou was right to urge surrender to Wei. He answers: For a reigning emperor to beg for his life— what deeper shame? One should die for the altars or perish with them. The First Lord denounced Wei's theft of the mandate and refused to share the sky with Cao Pi. To blame one's father and serve the foe is mere clinging to life, not the righteous path. Sun Sheng adds that the Spring and Autumn canon expects rulers to die for the state— how can a Son of Heaven endure humiliation? Sun Sheng concludes that Qiao Zhou urged a ruler of ten thousand chariots to cling to life without honor, chasing petty advantage— a deluded course. Even on pragmatic grounds, Sun Sheng's argument does not cover every case. Why? Liu Shan was a middling sovereign, not a monster like Jie or Zhou; though often defeated, his realm had not dissolved. Even if he could not hold Chengdu, he might have fallen back to the eastern garrisons and plotted recovery. Luo Xian still held Baidi with a strong force; Huo Yi still commanded Yelang. Shu is a maze of cliffs and rapids that infantry cannot easily cross. Seize the river fleet, fortify Jiangzhou, call up the southern tribes, and beg an expedition from Wu— then generals such as Jiang Wei would rally, Wu's armies would answer the call, and you would hardly be homeless wanderers awaiting doom. Wei's invasion strained the whole empire: to advance they lacked boats; to stay they risked a stalemate. Fortunes turn: rouse a desperate people against weary invaders, as Goujian beat Helü or Tian Dan broke Yan— why rush to surrender and hand the enemy a propaganda victory? The old song says, "If we fail, so be it— I will not live as their underling." Brave words— enough to stiffen a coward's spine. Ancient Yan, Qi, Chu, and Yue fell to ruin, yet their heirs rebuilt them— not heaven alone but human resolve. Had Liu Shan clung only to survival and heeded Zhou, what foundation or fame could he have won? A dull emperor and a plodding minister are poor company for the heroes who saved their states."

時晉文王為魏相國，以周有全國之功，封陽城亭侯。又下書辟周，周發至漢中，困疾不進。咸熙二年夏，巴郡文立從洛陽還蜀，過見周。周語次，因書版示立曰：「典午忽兮，月酉沒兮。」典午者謂司馬也，月酉者謂八月也，至八月而文王果崩。〈《華陽國志》曰：文立字廣休，少治毛詩、三禮，兼通羣書。刺史費禕命為從事，入為尚書郎，復辟禕大將軍東曹掾，稍遷尚書。蜀並於魏，梁州建，首為別駕從事，舉秀才。晉泰始二年，拜濟陰太守，遷太子中庶子。立上言：「故蜀大官及盡忠死事者子孫，雖仕郡國，或有不才，同之齊民為劇；又諸葛亮、蔣琬、費禕等子孫流徙中畿，各宜量才敘用，以慰巴、蜀之心，傾吳人之望。」事皆施行。轉散騎常侍，獻可替否，多所補納。稍遷衛尉，中朝服其賢雅，為時名卿。咸寧末卒。立章奏詩詩賦論頌凡數十篇。〉

When Sima Zhao was Wei's minister of state, he enfeoffed Zhou as marquis of Yangcheng for saving the Liu clan. Zhao summoned him again; Zhou reached Hanzhong but illness halted him. In the summer of Xianxi 2, Wen Li of Ba returned from Luoyang and called on Zhou. During their talk Zhou scribbled a riddle: "The steward of noon wanes" punned on the house of Sima; "the moon in you sets" pointed to the eighth month of the calendar. "Dianwu" punned on the house of Sima; "moon you" pointed to the eighth month— and Sima Zhao died that August. The Huayang Guo zhi names Wen Li as Guangxiu, trained in the Mao Odes, the three rituals, and general literature. Fei Yi made him adjutant, then a court secretary, then a staff officer under the grand general, and finally a director. After Shu fell he became chief clerk when Liangzhou was organized and was recommended as flourishing talent. In Taishi 2 of the Jin he became prefect of Jiyin, then junior tutor to the heir apparent. He memorialized that sons of Shu officials who had died for the state should not be lumped with commoners if untalented; and that the stranded heirs of Liang, Wan, and Yi deserved measured appointments to reassure Ba-Shu and impress Wu." The court adopted his proposals. He rose to supernumerary palace attendant and remonstrated effectively on policy. He ended as commandant of the guards, esteemed at court as a model minister. He died near the end of the Xianning era. He left several dozen memorials, poems, and essays.

晉室踐阼，累下詔所在發遣周。周遂輿疾詣洛，泰始三年至。以疾不起，就拜騎都尉，周乃自陳無功而封，求還爵土，皆不聽許。五年，予常為本郡中正，清定事訖，求休還家，往與周別。周語予曰：「昔孔子七十二、劉向、楊雄七十一而沒，今吾年過七十，庶慕孔子遺風，可與劉、楊同軌，恐不出後歲，必便長逝，不復相見矣。」疑周以術知之，假而此言也。六年秋，為散騎常侍，疾篤不拜，至冬卒。〈《晉陽秋》載詔曰：「朕甚悼之，賜朝服一具，衣一襲，錢十五萬。」周息熙上言，周臨終屬熙曰：「久抱疾，未曾朝見，若國恩賜朝服衣物者，勿以加身。當還舊墓，道險行難，豫作輕棺。殯斂已畢，上還所賜。」詔還衣服，給棺直。〉凡所著述，擇定《法訓》、《五經論》、《古史考》書之屬百餘篇。〈益部耆舊傳曰：益州刺史董榮圖畫周像於州學，命從事李通頌之曰：「抑抑譙侯，好古述儒，寶道懷真，鑑世盈虛，雅名美跡，終始是書。我後欽賢，無言不譽，攀諸前哲，丹青是圖。嗟爾來葉，鑑茲顯模。」〉

After the Jin accession, repeated edicts ordered Zhou to the capital. Zhou was carried to Luoyang ill and arrived in Taishi 3. Too ill to bow, he was named chief commandant of cavalry; he protested that he deserved no fief, but the throne refused. In the fifth year Pei Songzhi served as local impartial judge for his home commandery; when the roster work ended he visited Zhou to say goodbye. Zhou told him, "Confucius died at seventy-two, Liu Xiang and Yang Xiong at seventy-one. I am past seventy and hope to match their span— I doubt we shall meet again after next year." Songzhi suspected Zhou divined his end and spoke in riddles. In the sixth year's autumn he was named supernumerary palace attendant but was too ill to serve; he died that winter. The Jin Yang Autumn preserves an edict mourning him with robes and cash. His son Xi reported Zhou's deathbed wish that imperial gifts of dress not be placed on his corpse. He asked for a light coffin for the hard road home to his old grave. After the rites, return the gifts to the throne. The court returned the robes and paid for the coffin instead." His corpus includes over a hundred titles such as the Norms of Law, the Five Classics treatises, and the Investigations of Ancient History. The Yi elders' record tells how Inspector Dong Rong hung Zhou's portrait in the school and had Li Tong compose a hymn praising his scholarship and judgment. Our sovereign honors the worthy and sets their image in paint for posterity. O later generations, take this portrait as your mirror."
孫 譙秀
His grandson: Qiao Xiu.

周三子，熙、賢、同，少子同頗好周業，亦以忠篤質素為行，舉孝廉，除錫令、東宮洗馬，召不就。〈周長子熙。熙子秀，字元彥。《晉陽秋》曰：秀性清靜，不交於世，知將大亂，豫絕人事，從兄弟及諸親裡不與相見。州郡辟命，及李雄盜蜀，安車徵秀，又雄叔父驤、驤子壽辟命，皆不應。常冠鹿皮，躬耕山藪。永和三年，安西將軍桓溫平蜀，表薦秀曰：「臣聞大樸既虧，則高尚之標顯；道喪時昏，則忠貞之義彰。故有洗耳投淵以振玄邈之風，亦有秉心矯跡以惇在三之節。是以上代之君，莫不崇重斯軌，所以篤俗訓民，靜一流競。伏惟大晉應符禦世，運無常通，時有屯蹇，神州丘墟，三方圮裂，兔罝絕響於中林，白駒無聞於空谷，斯有識之所悼心，大雅之所嘆息者也。陛下聖德嗣興，方恢天緒。臣昔奉役，有事西土，鯨鯢既縣，思宣大化；訪諸故老，搜楊潛逸，庶武羅於羿、浞之墟，想王蠋於亡齊之境。竊聞巴西譙秀，植操貞固，抱德肥遁，揚清渭波。於時皇極遘道消之會，羣黎蹈顛沛之艱，中華有顧瞻之哀，幽谷無遷喬之望；凶命屢招，姦威仍偪，身寄虎吻，危同朝露，而能抗節玉立，誓不降辱，杜門絕跡，不面偽庭，進免龔勝亡身之禍，退無薛方詭之譏；雖園、綺之棲商、洛，管寧之默遼海，方之於秀，殆無以過。於今西土，以為美談。夫旌德禮賢，化道之所先，崇表殊節，聖哲之上務。方今六合未康，豺狼當路，遺黎偷薄，義聲弗聞，益宜振起道義之徒，以敦流遁之弊。若秀蒙薄帛之徵，足以鎮靜頹風，軌訓囂俗；幽遐仰流，九服知化矣。」及蕭敬叛亂，避難宕渠川中，鄉人宗族馮依者以百數。秀年八十，眾人以其薦老，欲代之負擔，秀拒曰：「各有老弱，當先營救。吾氣力自足堪此，不以垂朽之年累諸君也。」後十餘年，卒於家。〉

Zhou's three sons were Xi, Xian, and Tong. Tong followed his father's studies, earned recommendation as filial and incorrupt, was named magistrate of Xi and tutor to the heir, but refused the summons. Zhou's eldest son was Xi. Xi's son Qiao Xiu bore the courtesy name Yuanyan. The Jin Yang Autumn says Qiao Xiu was reclusive, foresaw chaos, broke off social ties, and would not even see kinsmen. He ignored every summons, including Li Xiong's carriage call and offers from Li Xiong's kinsmen. He wore a deerskin cap and farmed the hills in seclusion. In Yonghe 3, Huan Wen conquered Shu and recommended Xiu: "When simplicity is lost, recluses shine forth; when the age grows dark, steadfast loyalty stands out." Some fled the world to cleanse their ears; others held fast to duty to honor the three bonds." Ancient kings always honored such men to steady the people and quell strife. Great Jin rules a broken age: the heartland lies waste, the realm is split, worthies hide like the Book of Songs' lost hunters and white colts— a grief to every thoughtful man." Your Majesty renews the mandate of heaven. I once campaigned in the west; now that the rebels are cut down, I would extend your transforming influence; I sought old men and hidden talent as archers once hunted Yi and Zhuo, hoping to find another Wang Zhu among the lost." I hear that Qiao Xiu of Ba is incorruptible, virtuous, and reclusive as a clear stream. The throne totters, the people suffer, the heartland mourns, and no phoenix rises from the wilds; yet Xiu defies threats, shuts his gate, will not bow to usurpers, avoids Gong Sheng's suicide and Xue Fang's hypocrisy; he matches the recluses of Shang-Luo and Guan Ning at Liaodong— perhaps none surpass him." The west still tells his story with admiration. Honoring recluses is the first duty of moral government. With the realm still torn by wolves and the people cynical, you should lift up men of principle to cure flight from duty. A modest summons to Xiu would steady custom and shame the vulgar; the distant would look to your virtue and the nine provinces would feel your sway." When Xiao Jing rose in revolt, Xiu fled into the Dangqu valleys with hundreds of kinsmen. At eighty the refugees offered to carry his pack; he refused: "Everyone has elders to save first. I still have strength enough— do not waste it on an old man." He died at home more than a decade later."

郤正字令先，河南偃師人也。祖父儉，靈帝末為益州刺史，為盜賊所殺。會天下大亂，故正父揖因留蜀。揖為將軍孟達都督，隨達降魏，為中書令史。正本名纂。少以父死母嫁，單煢雙立，而安貧好學，博覽墳籍。弱冠能屬文，入為秘書吏，轉為令史，遷郎，至令。性淡於榮利，而尤耽意文章，自司馬、王、揚、班、傅、張、蔡之儔遺文篇賦，及當世美書善論，益部有者，則鑽鑿推求，略皆寓目。自在內職，與宦人黃皓比屋周旋，經三十年。皓從微至貴，操弄威權，正既不為皓所愛，亦不為皓所憎，是以宮不過六百石，而免於憂患。

Xi Zheng, courtesy name Lingxian, came from Yanshi in Henan. His grandfather Xi Jian was inspector of Yi Province under Emperor Ling and was killed by bandits. When the empire collapsed, his father Xi Yi stayed behind in Shu. Yi served as Meng Da's chief of staff, followed him to Wei, and became a secretariat clerk. Zheng had first been named Zuan. Orphaned when his father died and his mother remarried, he lived alone in poverty but read every classic he could find. He could write at twenty, joined the palace secretariat as a clerk, rose to secretary, then gentleman, and finally director. He cared little for rank but devoured literature, hunting down every essay by Sima Qian, Wang Chong, Yang Xiong, Ban Gu, Fu, Zhang, Cai Yong, and the best writers of his own day that could be found in Shu. For thirty years he worked next door to the eunuch Huang Hao. Hao rose from nothing to dominate the court; Zheng stayed beneath his notice and never rose above six hundred piculs yet avoided disaster.
依則先儒，假文見意，號曰：《釋譏》，其文繼於崔駰《達旨》。其辭曰：
He modeled his work on the Confucian masters and titled it Explaining Ridicule, in the tradition of Cui Yin's Expressing the Aim. It begins:

或有譏余者曰：『聞之前記，夫事與時並，名與功偕，然則名之與事，前哲之急務也。是故創製作範，匪時不立，流稱垂名，匪功不記，名必須功而乃顯，事亦俟時以行止，身沒名滅，君子所恥。是以達人研道，探頤索微，觀天運之符表，考人事之盛衰，辯者馳說，智者應機，謀夫演略，武士奮威，雲合霧集，風激電飛，量時揆宜，用取世資，小屈大申，存公忽私，雖尺枉而尋直，終揚光以發輝也。今三方鼎跱，九有未乂，悠悠四海，嬰丁禍敗，嗟道義之沉塞，愍生民之顛沛，此誠聖賢拯救之秋，烈士樹功之會也。吾子以高朗之才，珪璋之質，兼覽博窺，留心道術，無遠不致，無幽不悉；挺身取命，幹茲奧秘，躊躇紫闥，喉舌是執，九考不移，有入無出，〈《尚書》曰：三載考績，三考黜陟幽明。九考則二十七年。〉究古今之真偽，計時務得失。雖時獻一策，偶進一言，釋彼官責，慰此素餐，固未能輸竭忠款，盡瀝胸肝，排方入直，惠彼黎元，俾吾徒草鄙並有聞焉也。盍亦綏衡綏轡，回軌易塗，輿安駕肆，思馬斯徂，審歷揭以投濟，要夷庚之赫憮，播秋蘭以芳世，副吾徒之彼圖，不亦盛與！』余聞而歎曰：『嗚呼，有若雲乎邪！夫人心不同，實若其面，子雖光麗，既美且艷，管窺筐舉，守厥所見，未可以言八紘之形埒，信萬事之精練也。』或人率爾，仰而揚衡曰：『是何言與！是何言與！』」

A critic tells me: "The wise say fame must match deeds and the times—" so models fit the age and names follow achievement; to die forgotten shames a gentleman." The adept reads heaven and man, seizes the moment, bends when he must and straightens when he can, and ends in glory." Today the realm is a tripod of rivals, the people suffer— this is the hour for heroes to save the age." You have talent and character, study far and wide, bear office at court as spokesman, pass nine reviews without demotion, as the Documents says: three reviews in nine years set rank." Nine reviews mean twenty-seven years in office. You weigh past and present and judge policy. Yet an occasional memo hardly discharges your duty to the people or redeems a salary eaten in vain. Why not change course, ease your pace, choose a safer ford, plant virtue for the age, and meet the world's hopes?" I sighed, "What empty talk is this?" Hearts differ like faces; your pretty speech and narrow view cannot map the whole world." The man cried, "What words are these!" How can you say such a thing!"

余應之曰：「虞帝以面從為戒，孔聖以悅己為尤。若子之言，良我所思，將為吾子論而釋之。昔在鴻荒，朦昧肇初，三皇應菉，五帝承符，爰暨夏、商，前典攸書。姬衰道缺，霸者冀扶，嬴氏慘虐，吞嚼八區，於是從橫雲起，狙詐如星，奇衺蠭動，智故萌生；或飾真以仇偽，或挾邪以干榮，或詭道以要上，或鬻技以自矜；背正崇邪，棄直就佞，忠無定分，義無常經。故鞅法窮而慝作，斯義敗而姦成，呂門大而宗滅，韓辯立而身刑。夫何故哉？利回其心，寵耀其目，赫赫龍章，鑠鑠車服。偷幸苟得，如反如仄，淫邪荒迷，恣睢自極，和鸞未調而身在轅側，庭寧未踐而櫟折榱覆。天收其精，地縮其澤，人吊其躬，鬼芟其額。初升高岡，終隕幽壑，朝含榮潤，夕為枯魄。是以賢人君子，深圖遠慮，畏彼咎戾，超然高舉，寧曳屬於塗中，穢濁世之休譽。彼豈輕主慢民，而忽於時務哉？蓋《易》著行止之戒，《詩》有靖恭之歎，乃神之聽之而道使之然也。自我大漢，應天順民，政治之隆，皓若陽春，俯憲坤典，仰式乾文。播皇澤以熙世，揚茂化之酢醇，君臣覆度，各守厥真，上垂詢納之弘，下有匡救之責，士無虛華之寵，民有一行之跡，粲乎亹亹，尚此忠益。然而道有隆窳，物有興廢，有聲有寂，有光有翳。朱陽否於素秋，玄陰抑於孟春，羲和逝而望舒系，運氣匿而耀靈陳。沖、質不永，桓、靈墜敗，英雄雲布，豪傑蓋世，家挾殊議，人懷異計。故從橫者欻披其胸。狙詐者暫吐其舌也。

I replied, "Shun warned against flattery; Confucius condemned self-satisfaction. If that is your point, it is worth answering— hear me out." In primordial chaos the sage-kings answered heaven's signs; by Xia and Shang the pattern was already written in the classics. When Zhou decayed, the way broke; hegemons vied to shore it up; Qin devoured the realm; strategists and frauds swarmed like stars. Some masked greed as principle, some sold vice as virtue, some schemed for favor, some peddled cleverness; straight loyalty was abandoned for whatever won office. Hence Shang Yang's rigor bred cruelty, Li Si's "justice" bred treason, Lü Buwei's power destroyed his house, Han Fei's logic cost his life. Why? Profit blinded them, rank dazzled them— dragon badges, gleaming carriages. They snatched fortune like tipping a cart, raced into debauchery, and crashed before the bells of good rule ever rang. Heaven and earth withdrew favor; men and spirits marked them for ruin. They rose at dawn in splendor and by dusk were dry bones in the pit. So the wise feared disgrace, chose reclusion in the mire, and scorned hollow fame. They did not scorn ruler or people— they feared the times. The Book of Changes warns when to act or halt; the Odes praises quiet reverence— heaven hears such choices." Our Han answered heaven and the people; its golden age shone like spring; we took law from earth and pattern from sky. Ruler and minister shared one measure; the throne sought counsel, officials owed remonstrance; merit replaced puffery, and the realm thrived on plain duty. Yet every way waxes and wanes; every age knows light and shadow. The bright sun can fail in autumn frost; the dark moon can rule an early spring— cosmic breath shifts and the shining spirit shows or hides. Young emperors died young; Huan and Ling brought ruin; heroes clouded the land, each house nursing its own plot. The strategists tore their hearts open in debate. The sophists shot off clever talk.

今天綱已綴，德樹西鄰，丕顯祖之宏規，縻好爵於士人，興五教以訓俗，豐九德濟民，肅明祀以礿祭，幾皇道以輔真。雖跱者未一，偽者未分，聖人垂戒，蓋均無貧；故君臣協美於朝，黎庶欣戴於野，動若重規，靜若疊矩。濟濟偉彥，元凱之倫也，有過必知，顏子之仁也．侃侃庶政，冉、季之治也，鷹揚鷙騰，伊、望之事也；總羣俊之上略，含薛氏之三計，敷張、陳之秘策，故力徵以勤世，援化英而不遑，豈暇修枯籜於榛穢哉！然吾不才，在朝累紀，托身所天，心焉是恃。樂滄海之廣深，歎篙岳之高跱，聞仲尼之贊商，感鄉校之益己，彼平仲之和羹，亦近可而替否；故矇冒瞽說，時有攸獻，譬遒人之有採於市閭，遊童之吟詠乎疆畔，庶以增廣福祥，輸力規諫。若其合也，則以暗協明，進應靈符；如其違也，自我常分，退守己愚。進退任數，不矯不誣，循性樂天，夫何恨諸？此其所既入不出，有而若無者也。狹屈氏之常醒，濁漁父之必醉，溷柳季之卑等辱，編夷、叔之高懟。合不以得，違以不失，得不克詘，失不慘悸。不樂前以顧軒，不就後以慮輊，不鬻譽以乾澤，不辭愆以忌絀。何責之釋？何餐之卹？何方之排？何直之入？九考不移，固其所執也。方今朝士山積，髦俊成羣，猶鱗介之潛乎巨海，毛羽之集乎鄧林，游禽逝不為之鮮，浮魴臻不為之殷。且陽靈幽於唐葉，陰精應於商時，陽盱請而洪災息，桑林禱而甘澤滋。〈《淮南子》曰：禹為水，以身請於陽盱之河，湯苦旱，以身禱於桑林之際，聖人之憂民，如此其明也。《呂氏春秋》曰：昔殷湯克夏桀而天下大旱，三年不收，湯乃以身禱於桑林曰：「余一人有罪，無及萬方，萬方有罪，在余一人，無以一人之不敏，使上帝毀傷民之大命。」湯於是剪其髮，攦其爪，自以為犧牲，用祈福於上帝。民乃甚悅。雨乃大至。〉行止有道，啟塞有期。我師遺訓，不怨不尤，委命恭己，我又何辭？辭窮路單，將反初節，綜墳典之流勞，尋孔氏之遺藝，綴微辭以存道，儘先軌而投制，題叔肸之優遊，美疏氏之遐逝，收止足以言歸，泛皓然以容裔，欣環堵以恬娛，免咎悔於斯世，顧茲心之未泰，懼末塗之泥滯，仍求激而增憤，肆中懷以告誓。昔九方考精於至貴，秦牙沈思於殊形；〈《淮南子》曰：秦穆公謂伯樂曰：「子之年長矣，子姓有可使求馬者乎？」對曰：「良馬者，可以形容筋骨相也。相天下之馬者，若滅若沒，若失若亡，其一若此馬者，絕塵卻轍。臣之子皆下才也，可告以良馬而不可告以天下之馬。天下之馬，臣有所與共儋纏採薪九方堙，此其相馬，非臣之下也，請見之。」穆公見之，使之求馬，三月而反，報曰：「已得馬矣，在於沙丘。」穆公曰：「何馬也？」對曰：「牝而黃。」使人往取之，牡而驪。穆公不悅，召伯樂而問之曰：「敗矣，子之所使求馬者也！毛物牝牡尚弗能知，又何馬之能知？」伯樂喟然太息曰：「一至此乎！是乃所以千萬（里）臣而無數者也。若堙之所觀者天機也，得其精而忘其粗，在其內而忘其外，見其所見而不見其所不見，視其所視而遺其所不視，若彼之所相者，乃有貴乎馬者。」馬至，而果天下之馬也。淮南子又曰：伯樂、寒風、秦牙、葛青，所相各異，其知馬一也；蓋九方觀其精，秦牙察其形。〉薛燭察寶以飛譽，〈《越絕書》曰：昔越王句踐有寶劍五枚，聞於天下。客有能相劍者名薛燭，王召而問之：「吾有寶劍五，請以示子。」乃取豪曹、臣闕，薛燭曰：「皆非也。」又取純鉤、湛盧，燭曰：「觀其劍鈔，爛爛如列宿之行，觀其光，渾渾如水之將溢於塘，觀其文，渙渙如冰將釋，此所謂純鉤邪？」王曰：「是也。」王曰：「客有直之者，有市之鄉三，駿馬千匹，千戶之都二，可乎？」薛燭曰：「不可。當造此劍之時，赤堇之山破而出錫，若邪之谿涸而出銅，雨師掃灑，雷公擊鼓，太一下觀，天精下之，歐冶乃因天之精，悉其伎巧，一曰純鉤，二曰湛盧。今赤堇之山已合，若邪之谿深而不測，歐冶子已死，雖傾城量金，珠玉竭河，獨不得此一物。有市之鄉三，駿馬千匹，千戶之都二，亦何足言與！」〉瓠梁托弦以流聲；〈《淮南子》曰：瓠巴鼓瑟而鱘魚聽之。又曰：瓠梁之歌可隨也，而以歌者不可為也。〉齊隸拊髀以濟文，〈臣松之曰：按此謂孟嘗君田文下坐客，能作雞鳴以濟其厄者也。凡作雞鳴，必先拊髀，以傚雞之拊翼也。〉楚客潛寇以保荊：〈《淮南子》曰：楚將子發好求技道之士。楚有善為偷者，往見曰：「聞君求技道之士，臣偷也，原以技備一卒。」子發聞之，衣不及帶，冠不暇正，出見而禮之。左右諫曰：「偷者，天下之盜也，何為禮之？」君曰：「此非左右之所得與。」後無幾何，齊興兵伐楚。子發將師以當之，兵三卻。楚賢大夫皆盡其計而悉其誠，齊師愈強。於是卒偷進請曰：「臣有薄技，原為君行之。」君曰「諾」。偷即夜出，解齊將軍之帳，而獻之子發。子發使人歸之，曰：「卒有出採薪者，得將軍之帳，使使歸於執事。」明日又復往取枕，子發又使歸之。明日又復往取簪，子發又使歸之。齊師聞之大駭，將軍與軍吏謀曰：「今日不去，楚軍恐取吾頭矣！」即旋師而去。〉雍門援琴而挾說，〈桓譚《新論》曰：雍門周以琴見，孟嘗君曰：「先生鼓琴，亦能令文悲乎？」對曰：「臣之所能令悲者，先貴而後賤，昔富而今貧，擯壓窮巷，不交四鄰；不若身材高妙，懷質抱真，逢讒罹謗，怨結而不得信；不若交歡而結愛，無怨而生離，遠赴絕國，無相見期；不若幼無父母，壯無妻兒，出以野澤為鄰，入用堀穴為家，困於朝夕，無所假貸：若此人者，但聞飛烏之號，秋風鳴條，則傷心矣，臣一為之援琴而長太息，未有不淒惻而涕泣者也。今若足下，居則廣廈高堂，連闥洞房，下羅帷，來清風；倡優在前，諂諛侍側，揚激楚，舞鄭妾，流聲以娛耳，練色以淫目；水戲則舫龍舟，建羽旗，鼓釣乎不測之淵；野遊則登平原，馳廣囿，強弩下高鳥，勇士格猛獸；置酒娛樂，沈醉忘歸：方此之時，視天地曾不若一指，雖有善鼓琴，未能足下也。」孟嘗君曰：「固然！」雍門周曰：「然臣竊為足下有所常悲。夫角帝而困秦者君也，連五國而伐楚者又君也。天下未嘗無事，不從即衡；從成則楚王，衡成則秦帝。夫以秦、楚之強而報弱薛，猶磨蕭斧而伐朝菌也，有識之士，莫不為足下寒心。天道不常盛，寒暑更進退，千秋萬歲之後，宗廟必不血食；高台既已傾，曲池又已平，墳墓生荊棘，狐狸穴其中，遊兒牧豎躑躅其足而歌其上曰：『孟嘗君之尊貴，亦猶若是乎！』」於是孟嘗君喟然太息，涕淚承睫而未下。雍門周引琴而鼓之，徐動宮徵，叩角羽，終而成曲，孟嘗君遂歔欷而就之曰：「先生鼓琴，令文立若亡國之人也。」〉韓哀秉轡而馳名；〈《呂氏春秋》曰：韓哀作禦。王褒聖主得賢臣頌曰：及至駕齧膝，參乘旦，王良執靶，韓哀附輿，縱馳騁騖，忽如景靡，過都越國，蹶如歷塊，追奔電，逐遺風，周流八極，萬里一息，何其遼哉！人馬相得也。〉盧敖翱翔乎玄闕，若士竦身於雲清。〈《淮南子》曰：盧敖遊乎北海，經乎太陰，入乎玄闕，至於蒙轂之上，見一士焉，深目而玄準，戾頸而鳶肩，豐上而殺下，軒軒然方迎風而舞，顧見盧敖慢然下其臂，遯逃乎碑下。盧敖俯而視之，方卷龜殼而食合梨。盧敖乃與之語曰：「惟敖為背羣離黨，窮觀於六合之外者，非敖而已乎！敖幼而好遊，長不喻解，周行四極，惟北陰之不闚，今卒睹夫子於是，子殆可與敖為交乎！」若士者蠤然而笑曰：「嘻乎！子中州民，寧肯而遠至此？此猶光乎日月而戴列星，陰陽之所行，四時之所生，此其比夫不名之地，猶突奧也。若我南游乎罔{罒良}之野，北息於沈墨之鄉，西窮冥冥之黨，東貫鴻濛之光，此其下無地而上無天，聽焉無聞，視焉則眴，此其外猶有沈沈之汜，其餘一舉而千萬里，吾猶未能之在。今子遊始至於此，乃語窮觀，豈不亦遠哉！然子處矣，吾與汗漫期於九垓之上，吾不可以久。」若士舉臂而竦身，遂入雲中。盧敖仰而視之，弗見乃止，曰：「吾比夫子也，猶黃鵠之與壤蟲，終日行不離咫尺，自以為遠，不亦悲哉！」〉余實不能齊技於數子，故乃靜然守己而自寧。」

Today Wei has refastened heaven's net, planted virtue in the west, honors its founders, ennobles scholars, teaches the five relations, cultivates the nine virtues, tends the altars, and walks the kingly way. Though rivals remain and fraud still lurks, the sage's mean keeps the realm from starving. Court and countryside move in one compass, rest in one square. Great ministers throng like the Eight Yuans and Eight Kais; they own faults like Yan Hui, govern boldly like Ran Qiu, soar to duty like Yi Yin. They wield the best plans of Zhang Liang and Chen Ping— busy saving the age, they cannot fuss over dead letters in the weeds. I lack their gifts yet have served many years, trusting heaven and my sovereign. I love learning like the sea, revere virtue like a peak; Confucius praised Shang, the village school taught me; even Yan Ying's "harmonizing stew" can turn counsel to good. So I dare speak like a street collector of songs or a field child's rhyme— hoping to add some grain of luck and honest advice. If I am right, shadow meets light and heaven answers; if wrong, I keep my humble place and my silence. I advance or retire with fate, force nothing, lie about nothing, follow nature— why nurse a grudge? That is the "office entered but never left, duty done yet unseen." I would narrow Qu Yuan's wakefulness, cloud the fisherman's drunk wisdom, rank with Liu Xia's lowliness, yet match Boyi and Shu Qi's high scorn. I do not cling to success or flee failure; neither flattens nor terrifies me. I do not truckle to the chariot ahead or dread the one behind, hawk praise for favor, or dodge blame to keep a post. What duty have I shirked? What salary have I stolen? What upright path have I blocked? What crooked path have I taken? Nine reviews without shifting— that is my steadfast rule. The court teems with talent like fish in the sea or birds in the forest— one more voice neither crowds nor empties it. Sun and moon have their eclipses; Yu prayed at Yangxu and floods ended; Tang prayed at the mulberry grove and rain returned. The Huainanzi tells how Yu offered himself at Yangxu to stop floods and Tang at the mulberry grove to end drought— such was sage care for the people." The Lüshi Chunqiu records Tang's prayer after conquering Jie: "Blame me, not the people; if the people suffer, the fault is mine— do not let one dull ruler cost heaven its care for life." He cut his hair and nails and offered himself as a victim to heaven. The people rejoiced. The rains came in torrents. Action and rest follow the way; doors open and close in season. Confucius taught: blame neither heaven nor man; accept fate with humility— what answer need I add? When argument fails I return to the classics, follow Confucius' path in small phrases, envy the ease of Shu Xi and the flight of the hermits, hope to live content in a humble lane and escape this age's regrets— yet my heart is still uneasy, fearing the mire ahead, and I cry out this oath from my breast. Jiufang Gao read the spirit of horses; Qin Ya studied their bones; The Huainanzi: Duke Mu asked Bole for a successor to find horses. Bole replied, "A common good horse shows in bone and sinew. A horse of heaven seems absent yet outruns dust and ruts." My sons are middling; I can teach common steeds, not heaven's steeds. For heaven's horses use my cordwood-gatherer Jiufang Ying— his eye matches mine— send for him." Mu received him and sent him out; three months later he reported a horse at Sandy Hill. "What kind of horse?" Mu asked. "A yellow mare," he said. The groom brought back a black stallion. Mu was furious: "Your man is useless! He could not tell sex or color— how could he judge quality!" Bole sighed, "Has he truly reached that level! That is why he is worth ten thousand (leagues) of ordinary judges and still stands beyond count among them." Ying sees the spirit inside the beast and forgets hide and color— that is why he names heaven's horse." When the horse came, it was indeed the finest in the realm. The Huainanzi lists many judges— each used a different method yet grasped the same truth; Jiufang read the spirit, Qin Ya the body." Xue Zhu judged swords and won fame, the Yue jue shu tells how Goujian of Yue owned five famous blades. He summoned the connoisseur Xue Zhu to view them. He produced Haocao and Juque; Zhu said they were not the best. When shown Chunjun and Zhanlu he praised the starry edge, the watery gleam, the melting-ice grain— "This is Chunjun." The king agreed. The king offered three towns, a thousand horses, and two capitals of a thousand households for the sword. Zhu refused. He told how Ou Yezi forged them when heaven opened Mount Chijin for tin and dried Ruoye for copper, spirits sweeping and drumming while essence fell— making Chunjun and Zhanlu. Those mines are sealed, the smith is dead— no heap of gold or pearls can buy such a blade again. Your towns and horses are nothing beside it!" Hu Liang drew music from strings, the Huainanzi says Hu Ba's se charmed fish from the deep." It also says anyone may copy Hu Liang's tune, but no one can sing like Hu Liang." A Qi retainer slapped his thighs to mimic a cock and save his lord, Pei Songzhi notes this is the cock-crow guest who saved Lord Mengchang. Mimicking a cock begins with slapping the thigh like beating wings." A Chu thief slipped into camp to save the state, the Huainanzi tells how general Zi Fa of Chu loved odd talents. A thief offered his craft as a soldier's skill. Zi Fa rushed out half-dressed to honor him. His staff protested honoring a thief. He said, "You do not understand." Soon Qi invaded Chu. Zi Fa met them and fell back three times. Every Chu stratagem failed while Qi grew stronger. The thief stepped forward: "Let me use my small skill for you." The lord agreed. That night the thief slipped into the Qi camp, cut loose the general's tent hangings, and brought them to Zi Fa. Zi Fa sent them back with word that a foraging soldier had "found" the general's drapery and wished to return it politely. The next night he stole the pillow; again Zi Fa returned it. The third night he took the hairpin; again Zi Fa sent it back. The Qi army panicked; the council cried, "If we stay, Chu will have our heads!" They broke camp and fled." Yongmen Zhou plucked the zither and moved his hearer with argument, Huan Tan's New Discourses: Yongmen Zhou played for Lord Mengchang, who asked whether music could sadden him. Zhou listed the fallen noble, the ruined rich man, the recluse shunned by neighbors; the worthy slandered and disbelieved; lovers parted without quarrel across endless distance; the orphan with no kin, homeless between marsh and cave— such a man weeps at wind and birds; I have only to play and he floods with tears." But you, my lord, live in mansions hung with silk, cooled by breeze, with singers, sycophants, Chu melodies, Zheng dancers— every sense feasted; on water you race dragon boats under feather flags; on land you hunt the plain with crossbow and spear; you drink until heaven and earth seem smaller than your thumb— what player could sadden you?" Mengchang agreed. Zhou answered, "Yet I grieve for you nonetheless." You humbled Qin and led the league against Chu— the world never rests: vertical alliance or horizontal, one makes Chu king, the other makes Qin emperor." Against Qin or Chu, little Xue is a mushroom under an axe— every thinking man shudders for you. Heaven turns; after ages your line may no longer smell the smoke of sacrifice; your towers will fall, your pools fill in, thorns choke the tombs, and herd boys will sing over your bones, "So passed Lord Mengchang's glory!" Mengchang wept until tears hung on his lashes. Zhou played a slow, wrenching tune until Mengchang sobbed, "Your music has made me a man of a fallen kingdom." Han Ai mastered the chariot and won renown; the Lüshi Chunqiu credits Han Ai with the art of driving. Wang Bao's rhapsody praises Wang Liang and Han Ai: at dawn, whip in hand, they drive so fast they outrun wind and lightning across the realm— man and steed as one." So runs the praise of their perfect partnership." Lu Ao roamed the dark void; the transcendent leapt into the clouds; the Huainanzi tells how Lu Ao met a strange being in the far north who hid from him. Lu Ao peeked and saw him munching a pear on a tortoise shell. Lu boasted of his lonely travels beyond the world. He said he had seen every pole but the north and now begged friendship. The figure gave a cricket's laugh: "Ha!" "You are a townsman of the heartland— what brings you here?" "This place still has sun, moon, and seasons— beside the nameless void it is only a chimney nook." "I roam voids beyond north, south, east, and west where there is neither sky nor ground— vaster than you can leap in a thousand leagues— and I have not reached their limit." "You have barely started yet call yourself a traveler— presumptuous!" "Stay if you like; I am due to meet Hanman above the nine heavens— I cannot linger." He stretched and rose into the clouds. Lu Ao cried, "Beside him I am a mayfly beside a swan— pathetic!" I cannot match those masters; I keep still and find peace in myself."

景耀六年，後主從譙周之計，遣使請降於鄧艾。其書，正所造也。明年正月，鐘會作亂成都，後主東遷洛陽，時擾攘倉卒。蜀之大臣無冀從者，惟正及殿中督汝南張通，捨妻子單身隨侍。後主賴正相導宜適，舉動無闕，乃慨然歎息，恨知正之晚，時論嘉之。賜爵關內候。泰始中，除安陽令，遷巴西太守。泰始八年詔曰：「正昔在成都，顛沛守義，不違忠節，及見受用，盡心幹事，有治理之績，其以正為巴西太守。」咸寧四年卒。凡所著述詩論賦之屬，垂百篇。

In Jingyao 6 the Later Lord adopted Qiao Zhou's counsel and sent Deng Ai terms of surrender. Xi Zheng had drafted that letter. The next New Year Zhong Hui mutinied at Chengdu; the court moved east to Luoyang in chaos. No great officer chose exile with the sovereign except Xi Zheng and Zhang Tong, who abandoned their families to go. The Later Lord leaned on Zheng for deportment at the Wei court and sighed that he had known him too late; contemporaries praised them both. He was enfeoffed marquis within the passes. Under the Jin he became magistrate of Anyang, then prefect of Ba. A Taishi 8 edict cited his loyalty in Shu and his good work as prefect of Ba. He died in the fourth year of Xianning. His writings— verse, essays, rhapsodies— number nearly a hundred.

評曰：杜微脩身隱靜，不役當世，庶幾夷、皓之槩。周羣佔天有徵，杜瓊沈默慎密，諸生之純也。許、孟、來、李，博涉多聞，尹默精於左氏，雖不以德業為稱，信皆一時之學士。譙周詞理淵通，為世碩儒，有董、揚之規，郤正文辭燦爛，有張、蔡之風，加其行止，君子有取焉。二子處晉事少，在蜀事多，故著於篇。〈張璠以為譙周所陳降魏之策，蓋素料劉禪懦弱，心無害戾，故得行也。如遇忿肆之人，雖無他算，然矜殉鄙恥，或發怒妄誅，以立一時之威，快其斯須之意者，此亦夷滅之禍云。〉

Du Wei lived in seclusion like the ancient recluses. Zhou Qun read the sky truly; Du Qiong was reserved and exact— models of scholarly integrity. Xu Ci, Meng Guang, Lai Min, and Li were encyclopedic; Yin Mo mastered the Zuo commentary— none were famed as moral paragons, yet all were leading scholars. Qiao Zhou's learning matched Dong and Yang; Xi Zheng's prose matched Zhang and Cai— and their lives offer lessons worth keeping. Zhou and Zheng belong chiefly to Shu's story, so they fill this scroll. Zhang Fan argues Zhou knew Liu Shan too gentle to punish dissent, so surrender was safe.
